title: Evaluation

techniques.name: System-Level Eval
techniques.q: Did the agent get the job done?
techniques.what: Treat the agent as a black box. Give it a real task, let it run to completion, and check only the final result against the goal. This is the number stakeholders care about, and the one to gate releases on.
use: Release gates and regression checks before shipping a new prompt, model or tool
Comparing two agent versions on the same task set
Tasks with a checkable end state: tests pass, a record is updated, a file exists
metrics: share of tasks solved in all k repeated trials
p50 / p95 wall-clock time per task
turns taken; flags loops and waste
steps: Build a golden set of 50–200 realistic tasks, each with a verifiable end state
Write programmatic checkers for each end state wherever possible
Run every task several times, because agents are non-deterministic
Report success, pass^k, cost and latency together, never success alone
pitfalls: A pass says nothing about why. Pair it with process-level eval to debug
One lucky run hides flakiness, so use repeated trials
String-match checkers reject correct answers that are phrased differently
techniques.remember: Score the outcome, count the cost, repeat the run.
techniques.cap: Only the final state is checked. What happened inside the agent is out of scope.

techniques.name: Process-Level Eval
techniques.q: Where exactly did it go wrong?
techniques.what: Open the black box and score the trajectory: the plan, each tool call and its arguments, the order of steps, and how the agent recovered from errors. It turns a failed run into a specific fix.
use: Debugging failures that system-level eval surfaced
Tuning tool descriptions, prompts and planning logic
Catching agents that succeed wastefully through loops or redundant calls
metrics: right tool chosen at each step
exact, in-order or any-order vs a reference path
failed calls the agent retried or routed around
executed steps that follow the stated plan
steps: Instrument the agent so every step is a trace span (OpenTelemetry works well)
Define reference trajectories for key tasks, or a per-step rubric
Score each step with code checks first, then an LLM judge for judgment calls
Aggregate by step type to find the weakest link
pitfalls: Many paths can be valid, and exact-match scoring punishes good alternatives
Reference trajectories are costly to write and go stale when tools change
Step scores can look fine while the final outcome still fails
techniques.remember: Grade the path, not just the destination.
techniques.cap: Each step gets its own verdict, so the failure has an exact location.

cmp.needs: Traces + reference path or step rubric

techniques.name: LLM-as-a-Judge
techniques.what: A strong model grades outputs against a written rubric. It scales human-like judgment to thousands of cases for qualities code can’t check: helpfulness, tone, soundness of reasoning and policy compliance.
use: Open-ended outputs with no single right answer
Fast prompt iteration where human review would be the bottleneck
Continuous monitoring of sampled production traffic
metrics: score one output on pass/fail or a 1–5 scale
pick the better of outputs A and B
% agreement or Cohen’s κ on a labelled sample
steps: Write a rubric with concrete criteria and an example for each score
Ask the judge to reason first, then give the score
Prefer binary or 3-point scales, which are more consistent than 1–10
Label 50–100 cases by hand and check agreement before trusting the judge
pitfalls: Position bias: in pairwise mode, run both orders
Verbosity bias: longer answers score higher unless the rubric says otherwise
Self-preference: judge with a different model family where possible
techniques.remember: Rubric first, reasoning before score, calibrate against humans.
techniques.cap: The judge sees the output and the rubric, writes its reasoning, then scores.

techniques.name: Agent-as-a-Judge
techniques.q: Does the work really meet the spec?
techniques.what: The judge is itself an agent. It opens files, runs code, searches the workspace and reads the trajectory, then checks each requirement with evidence. The approach comes from the Agent-as-a-Judge paper (Zhuge et al., 2024) and its DevAI benchmark of 55 AI development tasks with 365 hierarchical requirements. There it agreed with human experts far more often than LLM-as-a-Judge, at a fraction of the cost of human review.
use: Long-horizon tasks that produce artifacts: codebases, reports, data pipelines
Requirements that can only be verified by running or inspecting something
Replacing costly expert review of complex deliverables
metrics: a requirement counts only if its prerequisites pass
verdicts backed by a file, output or log
steps: Break the task into explicit, checkable requirements
Give the judge read-only tools in a sandbox: file reader, code runner, search
Require an evidence citation for every verdict
Spot-check verdicts against human review on a sample
pitfalls: Slower and more expensive than a single LLM call
The judge agent makes its own mistakes, so audit it
It needs isolation so it can’t change what it evaluates
techniques.remember: Don’t just read the work. Inspect it and run it.
techniques.cap: The judge gathers evidence with tools before ruling on each requirement.

techniques.name: RAG Grounding Metrics
techniques.q: Is the answer backed by the sources?
techniques.what: Split retrieval-augmented generation into its two halves. Retrieval metrics ask whether the right context was found. Grounding metrics ask whether the answer stays within that context. A low score tells you which half to fix.
use: Any agent that answers from documents, a knowledge base or search results
Diagnosing hallucination: bad retrieval or bad generation?
Tuning chunk size, top-k, embeddings and re-rankers
metrics: supported claims ÷ total claims in the answer
how directly the answer addresses the question
relevant chunks ranked near the top
share of the reference answer covered by retrieved context
steps: Collect questions with reference answers, plus ideal source chunks if you can
Log the retrieved context alongside every answer
Score retrieval (precision, recall) and generation (faithfulness, relevancy) separately
Fix retrieval first when recall is low. Fix the prompt when faithfulness is low
pitfalls: Context recall needs ground-truth answers
An LLM extracts the claims, so scores carry judge noise
A faithful answer is still wrong if the source document is wrong
techniques.remember: Found the right context? Stayed inside it?
techniques.cap: Every claim must trace back to a retrieved chunk. Unsupported claims lower faithfulness.

cmp.needs: Logged context; gold answers for recall

techniques.name: Benchmark Suites
techniques.q: How does it compare with the field?
techniques.what: Public benchmark suites measure general agent capability on standard tasks with fixed harnesses. Use them to choose a model or framework. They are no substitute for an eval set built from your own tasks.
use: Shortlisting models or frameworks before you build
Tracking general capability across model upgrades
Reporting progress against a shared yardstick
metrics: 500 human-validated GitHub issues; the patch must pass the repo’s tests
466 real-world assistant questions over 3 difficulty levels
tool use with simulated users in retail and airline domains; reports pass^k
369 computer-use tasks on real desktop apps
Berkeley Function Calling Scoreboard: tool-call accuracy
steps: Pick the suites closest to your agent’s work: code, web, tools or desktop
Run the official harness and settings so results are comparable
Report pass@1, cost and run time, not just the headline score
Mirror the format in a private set built from your own tasks
pitfalls: Contamination: test items may be in the model’s training data
Saturation: top scores stop separating strong systems
Scoreboard setups often differ from your production constraints
techniques.remember: Benchmarks to choose, private evals to ship.
techniques.cap: Which capabilities each benchmark exercises. Choose the ones that match your agent’s job.

techniques.name: Eval Datasets
techniques.q: Is the test set itself worth trusting?
techniques.what: Build and maintain the set of cases every other evaluation runs on. Cases come from production logs, support tickets and subject experts; they are stratified by intent, language and risk, topped up with edge, adversarial and reviewed synthetic cases, labelled against a rubric by two people, sized for the confidence you need, versioned, and refreshed from new failures. The scoring methods live in the other techniques here; this one is about the data they score.
use: Before trusting any release gate, judge or benchmark comparison on your own tasks
When scores look good but users still report failures the set never shows
When a new language, intent or product line reaches production
metrics: intents, languages and risk tiers with enough cases to score
≈ 1.96 · √(p(1 − p) ÷ n) around the measured rate
% agreement and Cohen’s κ between two annotators
share of gold labels that are wrong after review
share of cases drawn from the last one or two releases
cases never used while tuning prompts, kept for the final check
steps: Sample real traffic, tickets and expert cases; redact personal data first
Stratify by intent, language and risk, with a floor per stratum and adversarial cases
Label with a written rubric: two annotators, measure agreement, adjudicate disagreements
Size for the margin you need, version the set, hold some back, and add each new failure
pitfalls: Synthetic-only sets look easy and clean, so scores come out high and miss real traffic
Tuning prompts against the same cases over and over overfits the set
Too few cases per slice: a 4-point drop hides inside a ±5-point margin
techniques.remember: Real cases, every slice, two labellers, enough n, and refresh from failures.
techniques.cap: Illustrative: Suraksha General, a fictional Indian insurer, building the test set for its claims assistant.

cmp.scope: The test cases and their labels
cmp.needs: Production samples, a rubric and annotator time

techniques.name: User Simulation for Multi-Turn Agents
techniques.q: Does the agent still work when the user talks back?
techniques.what: A single-turn test gives the agent everything at once. Real users reveal details slowly, change their mind, write in Hinglish, get impatient and make mistakes. User simulation has an LLM play the user from a scenario card: a persona, a goal, details it knows but reveals only when asked, and rules for when to stop. The simulated user and the agent talk for many turns, and the conversation is scored on the end state (was the refund raised, with the right amount) plus a rubric. Because both sides are stochastic, each scenario runs k times and reliability is reported as pass^k, the chance that all k runs succeed. Building the scenario set is covered by Eval Datasets; this technique is the multi-turn harness.
use: Customer support and booking agents that gather details over several turns
Checking behaviour with difficult personas before real users meet them
Regression tests for multi-turn policies such as refunds and KYC
metrics: persona, goal, hidden details, stop rule and the expected end state
reveal details only when asked, stay in character, never solve the task for the agent
compare database or tool state with the expected one, not the transcript wording
probability all k runs of a scenario succeed; falls fast when agents are inconsistent
language, patience, expertise, mistakes; weighted like the real user base
the LLM user breaking character or leaking hidden details; audit a sample
steps: Write scenario cards from real conversations, with hidden details and expected end state
Prompt a simulator model to play the user, with rules against leaking or solving
Run each scenario k times and check end states in the backend
Report pass^1 and pass^k by persona, and read failed transcripts
pitfalls: Scripted user turns that never react to the agent, so every test passes
A simulator that reveals every detail in its first message, making the task easy
Only polite English personas when real users write in Hinglish and in a hurry
techniques.remember: An LLM plays the user; check the end state; repeat and report pass^k.
techniques.cap: Illustrative: Paisa Setu, a fictional UPI app, tests its refund agent on 200 simulated conversations.

techniques.name: Pairwise Comparison and Statistical Significance
techniques.q: Is version B really better, or is it noise?
techniques.what: When two versions of a prompt, model or agent are compared, the question is not “what score did B get” but “how often is B better than A on the same inputs, and could that be chance”. Pairwise comparison shows a judge (human or LLM) both answers to each question and asks which is better, in both orders to cancel position bias. The result is a win rate with a confidence interval; if the interval includes 50%, the data cannot tell the versions apart. Sample size sets the interval width, so it is chosen before running. Many versions can be ranked with a Bradley–Terry or Elo model fitted to pairwise results. Writing good rubrics and calibrating judges is covered by LLM-as-a-Judge; this technique is about comparing and deciding.
use: Deciding whether to ship a new prompt, model or retrieval change
Ranking several candidate models on your own tasks
Reporting eval results with error bars instead of single numbers
metrics: share of paired questions where B beats A, ties counted as half
judges often favour the first or second slot; run both orders and count split verdicts as ties
about ±1.96 × √(p(1−p)/n); about ±3.5 points at n=800 and ±7 at n=200
ship only if the lower bound is above 50%, or a paired test gives p below your threshold
decide in advance from the smallest gain worth detecting
turn many pairwise results into a ranking with uncertainty
steps: Fix the question set and the smallest improvement worth shipping
Generate answers from A and B on the same questions
Judge each pair in both orders; count split verdicts as ties
Report the win rate with a 95% interval and ship only if it clears 50%
pitfalls: Showing B always in the same slot, so position bias decides the result
Peeking at results and stopping as soon as B looks ahead
Comparing two separate average scores instead of paired outcomes on the same questions
techniques.remember: Same questions, both orders, a win rate with an interval; ship only if it clears 50%.
techniques.cap: Illustrative: Kaveri Bank, a fictional bank, compares a new prompt for its loan-query assistant against the current one.

import statistics, time

TASKS = load_golden_set("golden_tasks.jsonl")        #@1
K = 3                                                 #@1,2

results = []
for task in TASKS:                                    #@2
    for trial in range(K):                            #@2
        start = time.time()                           #@2
        run = agent.run(task.input)                   #@2
        results.append({
            "task": task.id,
            "ok": task.check(run.final_state),        #@3
            "cost": run.cost_usd,                     #@2
            "secs": time.time() - start,              #@2
        })

ok = [r["ok"] for r in results]                       #@4
success = sum(ok) / len(ok)                           #@4
by_task = {t.id: [r["ok"] for r in results if r["task"] == t.id] for t in TASKS}   #@4
pass_k = sum(all(v) for v in by_task.values()) / len(TASKS)                       #@4
cost_per_success = sum(r["cost"] for r in results) / max(sum(ok), 1)              #@4
p95 = statistics.quantiles([r["secs"] for r in results], n=20)[18]                #@4

assert success >= 0.90 and p95 < 8, "release blocked"   #@5
steps: Build a golden set
Collect 50–200 real tasks. Each needs an end state that code can check: a database row, a file, a passing test.
Run every task several times
Agents are non-deterministic, so run each task K times (3–5 is typical). Record cost and wall-clock time for every run.
Check the end state, not the wording
A checker function inspects the final state. Two runs pass; one leaves the order in the wrong status and fails.
Aggregate the metrics
Success rate averages all runs. pass^k counts tasks that passed every run. Add cost per success and p95 latency.
Gate the release
Ship only if every threshold holds. Here success is 0.87, below 0.90, so this version is blocked.

names the damage, and invents nothing.                       #@1

def judge(case) -> int:                                        #@2
    prompt = (RUBRIC + f"\nInput: {case.input}\nOutput: {case.output}\n"   #@2
              "Explain your reasoning, then end with SCORE: 0 or 1.")      #@3
    reply = llm(prompt, model=JUDGE_MODEL, temperature=0)      #@2

def pairwise(a, b) -> str:                                     #@4
    ab = judge_pair(first=a, second=b)    # "first" or "second"   #@4
    ba = judge_pair(first=b, second=a)                         #@4
    if ab == "first" and ba == "second": return "a"            #@4
    if ab == "second" and ba == "first": return "b"            #@4
    return "tie"                          # order changed the verdict   #@4

from sklearn.metrics import cohen_kappa_score                  #@5

import math, random
from collections import defaultdict
from sklearn.metrics import cohen_kappa_score

logs = load_logs("claims-assistant", since="2026-03-01")                 #@1
logs = [redact(x, fields=("name", "phone", "policy_no", "aadhaar")) for x in logs]  #@1

TARGET, FLOOR = 180, 3                                                    #@2
by_stratum = defaultdict(list)                                            #@2
for x in logs:                                                            #@2
    by_stratum[(x["intent"], x["lang"], x["risk"])].append(x)             #@2

rng, cases = random.Random(7), []
for key, group in by_stratum.items():                                     #@2
    k = max(FLOOR, round(TARGET * len(group) / len(logs)))                #@2
    picked = rng.sample(group, min(k, len(group)))                        #@2
    if len(picked) < FLOOR:                                               #@3
        picked += sme_review(synthesise(key, FLOOR - len(picked)))  # kept only if approved  #@3
    cases += picked
cases += load_jsonl("adversarial_v3.jsonl")   # 20: injected PDFs, fake claim ids  #@3

a = [label(c, rubric=RUBRIC, annotator="A") for c in cases]               #@4
b = [label(c, rubric=RUBRIC, annotator="B") for c in cases]               #@4
print(cohen_kappa_score(a, b))                                            #@4
gold = [x if x == y else adjudicate(c, x, y) for c, x, y in zip(cases, a, b)]  #@4

def margin(p, n):                                                         #@5
    return 1.96 * math.sqrt(p * (1 - p) / n)                              #@5

print(f"±{margin(0.85, 180):.1%}")        # ±5.2%: too wide for a 4-point drop  #@5

holdout = rng.sample(range(len(cases)), k=len(cases) // 5)               #@6
save_dataset("claims-eval", version="v4", cases=cases, labels=gold, holdout=holdout)  #@6
# monthly: add_cases("claims-eval", pull_failures(since="v4"))           #@6
steps: Start from real traffic

Sample six months of the claims assistant's conversations, plus support tickets and the cases claims officers say go wrong. Redact names, phone numbers, policy numbers and Aadhaar numbers before anyone reads them. The helpers here (load_logs, redact, label and so on) are stubs for your own code.
Stratify, with a floor

Group the logs by intent, language and risk, and sample each group in proportion to its traffic, but never fewer than 3 cases. Proportional sampling alone would give a 1% intent such as a death claim about 2 cases out of 180; the floor keeps rare but costly intents in the set.
Fill gaps carefully

Where a stratum has fewer than 3 real cases, synthetic cases fill the gap, and each is kept only if a subject expert approves it. 20 adversarial cases are added on purpose: a claim PDF with hidden instructions, a claim number that does not exist, abusive Hinglish. They are scored as their own slice.
Label twice, then adjudicate

Two annotators grade all 200 cases against the same written rubric. They disagree on 24: 88% agreement, but Cohen's κ is only about 0.53, because most answers are correct and agreement on those is easy. A senior claims officer settles each disagreement, and unclear rubric lines are rewritten.
Size for the margin you need

At 85% accuracy on 180 production-like cases the 95% margin is 1.96 × √(0.85 × 0.15 ÷ 180) ≈ ±5.2 points. A real 4-point regression disappears inside that. Comparing two versions needs more, about 900 cases for a margin of ±2.3 on each score.
Version, hold out, refresh

Save the set as v4 with the labels, and keep a fifth of it as a holdout that nobody looks at while tuning prompts. Every month, add the new production failures, so the set follows the traffic instead of last year's.

steps: Write a scenario card
Paisa Setu, a fictional UPI app, writes cards from real chats: a persona, a goal, hidden details such as the UTR number, and the expected end state in the backend.
Give the simulator rules
The simulated user must stay in character, reveal details only when asked and never solve the task. Without these rules it pastes everything in the first message and the test is too easy.
Let them talk
The simulator and the agent exchange turns until the simulator says DONE or 12 turns pass. The agent has to ask for the UTR number, confirm the amount and raise the ticket.
Check the end state
Success is a refund ticket for ₹2,450 in the backend, not polite wording in the transcript.
Repeat each scenario
Each of 200 scenarios runs 4 times. pass^1 is the average success; pass^4 counts scenarios where all 4 runs succeed.
Read the numbers
With a realistic mix of personas, pass^1 is 71% (scripted tests said 95%) and pass^4 is only 25%: the agent is right most of the time but not reliably.

    second = judge(q, b, a)           # same pair, swapped                #@3
    if first == "2" and second == "1": return 1.0      # B wins both

    return 0.5                                          # split: a tie     #@3

steps: Fix the question set first
Kaveri Bank, a fictional bank, samples 800 real loan queries before looking at any results, so it cannot pick questions that flatter the new prompt.
Answer the same questions
Both versions answer every question. Paired answers remove the difference in difficulty between questions.
Judge in both orders
Its judge prefers the first slot by about 10 points. Each pair is judged as A,B and as B,A; if the verdicts disagree, the pair is a tie.
Compute the win rate
B wins 56% of pairs, ties counted as half.
Add the interval
±1.96 × √(0.56 × 0.44 ÷ 800) ≈ ±3.4 points, so 53% to 59%. The whole interval is above 50%: ship.

import math
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.metrics import cohen_kappa_score
from statsmodels.stats.proportion import proportion_confint, samplesize_confint_proportion

logs = pd.read_parquet("claims_logs_redacted.parquet")   # intent, lang, risk, text

# 1. Stratified sample with a floor of 3 per stratum
TARGET, FLOOR = 900, 3
parts = []
for _, group in logs.groupby(["intent", "lang", "risk"]):
    k = max(FLOOR, round(TARGET * len(group) / len(logs)))
    parts.append(group.sample(min(k, len(group)), random_state=7))
sample = pd.concat(parts)
print(sample.groupby("lang").size())            # check the Hindi slice

# 2. Agreement between two annotators on the same cases
a = pd.read_csv("labels_a.csv")["verdict"]      # pass / fail per case
b = pd.read_csv("labels_b.csv")["verdict"]
print("agreement", (a == b).mean(), "kappa", round(cohen_kappa_score(a, b), 2))

# 3. How sure is the score? 765 of 900 correct = 85%
low, high = proportion_confint(count=765, nobs=900, alpha=0.05, method="wilson")
print(f"85.0% (95% CI {low:.1%} to {high:.1%})")

# 4. How many cases for a ±2-point margin at 85%?
n = samplesize_confint_proportion(proportion=0.85, half_length=0.02, alpha=0.05)
print(math.ceil(n))                              # 1,225 cases

import anthropic
from my_agent import respond, backend        # your agent and backend check

client = anthropic.Anthropic()

lib: binomtest gives an exact sign test and a confidence interval for the win rate.
code:
import json
from scipy.stats import binomtest

rows = [json.loads(l) for l in open("verdicts.jsonl")]   # {"ab": "2", "ba": "1"} per pair
wins = sum(r["ab"] == "2" and r["ba"] == "1" for r in rows)
losses = sum(r["ab"] == "1" and r["ba"] == "2" for r in rows)
ties = len(rows) - wins - losses

win_rate = (wins + 0.5 * ties) / len(rows)
test = binomtest(wins, wins + losses, 0.5)
ci = test.proportion_ci(confidence_level=0.95)
print(f"win rate {win_rate:.1%}; ties {ties}; decisive-pair CI {ci.low:.1%}-{ci.high:.1%}; p={test.pvalue:.4f}")

system.title: pass^k for each task
system.explain: This averages the runs, which is the success rate, not pass^k. pass^k counts a task only if every run passed, so T1 above should contribute 0, not 0.67.

process.title: In-order trajectory match
process.explain: “step not in actual” searches the whole list each time, so order is never checked. This is an any-order match: [get_account, find_order, issue_refund] would wrongly pass.

llmjudge.title: A pass/fail judge
llmjudge.explain: temperature=1.0 makes the judge sample randomly, so the same output can pass on one run and fail on the next. Judges should run at temperature 0 so scores are repeatable.

also.5: Parsing the last character is fragile, but it isn’t the planted bug: it works when the model follows the format.

agentjudge.title: Setting up the judge’s sandbox
agentjudge.code:
sandbox = Sandbox(image="python:3.12", repo="/work",
                  read_only=False, network=False)
tools = [sandbox.read_file, sandbox.run]

for req in REQUIREMENTS:
    verdict[req] = judge_agent(task=req, tools=tools,
                               must_cite_evidence=True)
agentjudge.explain: read_only=False lets the judge change the work it is grading: it could “fix” a failing file and then pass it. Mount the work read-only.

rag.title: Computing faithfulness
rag.explain: Faithfulness asks whether each claim is supported by the retrieved chunks. Checking against the reference answer measures correctness instead, and hides hallucinations that happen to be true.
rag.fix: supported = [c for c in claims if is_supported(c, chunks)]

bench.title: Comparing models on cost
bench.code:
models = {"Alpha": (0.60, 0.41), "Beta": (0.15, 0.47)}  # (cost per task, resolve rate)

for name, (cost, rate) in models.items():
    cost_per_resolved = cost * rate
    print(f"{name}: ${cost_per_resolved:.2f} per resolved task")
bench.explain: Multiplying makes a worse model look cheaper. Cost per resolved task is cost ÷ resolve rate: Alpha is $0.60 ÷ 0.41 ≈ $1.46, not $0.25.

evaldata.title: Stratified sample without a floor
evaldata.explain: Pure proportional allocation rounds small strata down to nothing. A Hindi death-claim stratum with 0.2% of traffic gets round(180 × 0.002) = round(0.36) = 0 cases, so the rarest and most sensitive claims never appear in the test set. Give every stratum a floor, and reweight to the traffic mix when you report the overall score.

also.2: Correct: a fixed seed makes the sample reproducible, so the set can be rebuilt exactly.
also.9: Correct: min() stops sample() from asking for more cases than a small stratum holds.

usersim.title: Scoring simulated conversations
usersim.explain: The agent saying the word “refund” does not mean a refund ticket exists. Agents often promise actions they never take. Success must be checked in the backend state.

also.2: Giving the simulator its rules on the first message is right.
also.6: Stopping on DONE, with a turn limit, is right.

pairwise.title: Pairwise verdicts
pairwise.explain: The judge only ever sees A first. Its first-slot bias is counted as a loss for B, so a genuinely better B can look worse.
pairwise.fix:
first, second = judge(q, a, b), judge(q, b, a)
    return 1.0 if (first, second) == ("2", "1") else 0.0 if (first, second) == ("1", "2") else 0.5

also.3: Mapping "2" to a B win is right for the A,B order.
also.5: Returning a number per pair is right; the win rate is their mean.

2: The agent now runs each golden task. How many times?
Once: the golden set is fixed, so one run is enough
Several times, because agents are non-deterministic
The same task can pass on one run and fail on the next. Several runs expose that flakiness.
3: How do we decide whether a run passed?
Compare the agent's final message with an expected sentence
Check the final state in code: database, files, tests
Wording varies between runs; the end state is what matters and can be checked exactly.
4: A task passed 2 of 3 runs. Does it count toward pass^3?
Yes: it passed most runs
No: pass^3 needs every run to pass
pass^3 counts only tasks that passed all three runs. That's what makes it a reliability measure.
5: Success is 0.87 and the threshold is 0.90. What happens?
The release ships with a warning
The release is blocked
A gate is a hard rule. Below threshold means blocked, no matter how close.

2: To score the trace, what do we compare it against?
A reference path of the steps a correct run needs
The final answer text
Process-level eval compares steps with a reference path, or scores them with a rubric.
3: The trace has one extra get_account call. Does the in-order match pass?
Yes: extra steps are allowed if the reference steps appear in order
No: any extra step fails it
In-order match allows extras. Only the exact match fails on an extra call.
4: 3 steps were needed and 4 were taken. What's the efficiency?
Efficiency = needed ÷ taken = 3 ÷ 4 = 0.75.
5: The refund went out in USD. Would a system-level check catch it if a refund record exists?
Probably not: the end state says a refund happened
Yes, always
That's why argument checks matter: the outcome can look right while a step is wrong.
6: What do we do with step-level findings?
Aggregate by tool across many traces and fix the weakest tool
Fix each trace one at a time
Patterns across traces point to the tool description or prompt that needs changing.

2: Which model should do the judging?
The same model that produced the output
A strong model, ideally from a different family, at temperature 0
A different family reduces self-preference; temperature 0 makes scores repeatable.
3: Should the judge give the score first or reason first?
Score first, then explain
Reason first, then give the score
Reasoning first produces more considered scores and an audit trail.
4: When comparing A and B, what guards against position bias?
Judge both orders and count a win only if they agree
Always show the better answer first
If the verdict flips with the order, it isn't a real preference.
5: How do we know the judge is trustworthy?
Compare its labels with a hand-labelled sample
Trust it if its reasoning sounds convincing
Convincing reasoning can still be wrong. Measure agreement, and Cohen's κ, against people.

2: How should the agent's work be exposed to the judge?
Read-only, in a sandbox with no network
With write access so the judge can fix issues
The judge must never change what it grades.
3: What must every verdict include?
Evidence such as a file, command output or log
Just pass or fail
Evidence lets a person check a verdict in seconds.
4: R2 failed. R3 depends on R2 and looks fine on its own. What's R3's verdict?
Pass
Blocked
A requirement can't count if something it depends on failed.
5: 1 of 3 requirements passed. What's the score?
1 ÷ 3 ≈ 0.33. R3 is blocked, not passed.

2: The model writes an answer from the chunks. Is it automatically grounded?
Yes: it was given the chunks
Not necessarily: it can still add unsupported claims
Models can add details that no chunk supports. That's what faithfulness measures.
3: 3 claims, 2 supported by the chunks. What's the faithfulness?
4: Context recall compares the retrieved chunks with…
The reference answer's facts
The model's answer
Recall asks whether retrieval found everything the correct answer needs.
5: Recall is low. Which half do you fix first?
Retrieval
Generation
A model can't cite what it was never given.

2: What does the agent produce for each issue?
A patch (diff) for the repository
A written explanation of the fix
SWE-bench grades patches by running tests, not prose.
3: Why build a Docker environment per repository?
So results are reproducible with the right dependencies
To make the agent faster
Each repository needs its own versions of dependencies to run its tests.
4: A patch fixes the issue but breaks another test. Is it resolved?
Yes
No: PASS_TO_PASS tests must still pass
Resolved means the issue is fixed and nothing else broke.
5: Model X tops the scoreboard. Ship it?
Yes
Confirm on your own issues first
Scoreboards shortlist; your own tasks decide.

2: Death claims are 1% of traffic. With 180 cases sampled purely in proportion, how many death claims would you expect?
About 2, so a floor of 3 per stratum is needed
About 18, plenty to score
1% of 180 is 1.8. Proportional sampling alone leaves rare but costly intents with almost nothing to score.
3: A stratum has only 1 real case. What fills the gap?
Synthetic cases, used straight from the generator
Synthetic cases kept only after a subject expert approves each one
Generated cases are often easier and cleaner than real ones. Expert review keeps only the realistic ones.
4: Two annotators agree on 88% of cases. Is that strong agreement?
Yes: 88% is high
Not necessarily: most answers are correct, so chance agreement is high; κ is about 0.53
When 85% of answers are correct, two people agree often by chance. Cohen’s κ corrects for that.
5: At 85% accuracy and 180 cases the margin is about ±5.2 points. Can this set show a real 4-point drop?
Yes: 4 points is a real change
No: the drop is smaller than the uncertainty
A 4-point change inside a ±5.2 margin on each score cannot be told apart from noise.
6: The team tunes prompts against the full set for a month and the score climbs 6 points. What protects you?
A holdout nobody tuned on, checked at the end
Re-running the same set three times
Tuning against the same cases overfits them. A holdout shows whether the gain carries over.

Share every detail in its first message
Refuse to talk
Then the agent never has to ask.

The simulated user never gives it, and the refund fails
The simulator gives it anyway
Hidden details come only when asked.

Pass

Pairing removes differences in question difficulty
To double the cost
Each pair shares the same difficulty.

A tie
A wins
It followed the slot, not the answer.

Ship B
Not proven

A strong model scores each output.
Check agreement with human labels before trusting it.

It checks the work requirement by requirement.

system: Your order-status agent resolves 47 of 50 replayed tickets on a single run. The support head wants to ship on Friday. What do you do first?
Replay each ticket 3–5 times and gate on pass^k
Add 50 more tickets and run them once
One run can pass by luck. Repeating each ticket shows which ones work every time, which is what customers experience.
A refund agent says “Your refund is done.” Which checks prove the refund really happened? Select all that apply.
The order status in the database is “refunded”
The refunded amount in the payments table matches the policy
An audit-log entry exists for the refund
End-state checks inspect real systems. The reply can say “refunded” when nothing happened.
A rebooking agent is replayed 3 times on 3 disruption cases. Case A passes 3/3, B passes 2/3, C passes 0/3. What is pass^3?
pass^3 counts a case only if all three runs passed. Only A did: 1 ÷ 3 ≈ 0.33.
Same results (A 3/3, B 2/3, C 0/3). The product manager puts pass@3 in the release note. What number is that, and what is the problem?
0.67, but it counts cases that passed at least once, while each customer gets one run
0.33, and it is the right number to publish
pass@3 = 2 ÷ 3 ≈ 0.67. It is optimistic: a customer gets one attempt, not the best of three.
You are writing the release gate for a plan-change agent. What belongs in it? Select all that apply.
Number of lines in the system prompt
Gate on what customers and the business feel: quality, cost and speed.
Version 2 of a claims agent keeps 92% success, but cost per successful claim rises from $0.04 to $0.11. What does this show?
A cost regression the gate should catch
Nothing: cost is not part of evaluation
Nearly 3× the cost for the same quality is a regression. Put cost in the gate.
You are building the golden set for an appointment-booking agent. Where should the tasks come from?
Real, anonymized patient requests plus past failures
Real traffic and known failures make the set representative of what the agent will face.
A dispute agent passes 95% of golden tasks, yet operations found it opened duplicate dispute tickets in 4% of runs that still ended “resolved”. Why did the gate miss it?
It checked only the final status, not side effects along the way
Outcome checks miss harmful steps. Add a “no duplicate tickets” end-state check and score the trace with process-level eval.
Why run golden tasks against a sandboxed copy of production data?
So checkers can inspect realistic end states without touching real customers
You need realistic state to check, without real money moving or real customers affected.
The same checkout-help task passes on some runs and fails on others, and the failing runs are the ones where the sandbox payment API happened to be slow. What kind of problem is this?
It works sometimes and fails sometimes depending on conditions. That is flakiness, and repeated trials expose it.
Your KYC agent’s test suite was written six months ago. Live complaints are about cases the suite never covered. What is the fix?
Keep the suite frozen so scores stay comparable
Add recent complaint cases to the golden set and keep growing it as a regression set
Test only with a public benchmark
A golden set is a living asset. Every production failure should become a new test case.
The checker for a password-reset task passes if the reply contains “reset link sent”. What is wrong with it?
Nothing: it is a clear check
It passes even if no email was sent; check the email outbox or audit record instead
It should use an LLM judge
Check the state change (an email queued for that user), not what the agent says it did.
A delivery-query agent averages 4 s per answer, but p95 is 19 s. The goal is that 95% of customers get an answer within 10 s. Does it pass?
Yes: the average is well under 10 s
No: p95 is 19 s, so more than 5% of customers wait over 10 s
Yes, if the success rate is high
Averages hide the slow tail. Gate on the percentile the goal is written in.
A prior-authorization agent has pass^1 = 0.90 and pass^5 = 0.62. What does that tell you?
Many tasks succeed only some of the time, so it has a consistency problem
pass^5 is always lower, so ignore it
The golden set is too small
If every task passed 90% of runs, pass^5 would be about 0.9⁵ ≈ 0.59. So failures are spread across many tasks: reliability, not capability, is the problem.
Two prompt versions score 88% and 90% on a 50-task set, one run each. Can you say version 2 is better?
Yes: 2 points is a clear win
No: 2 points is one task, which is within run-to-run noise; add trials or tasks
Yes, if the model is the same
On 50 tasks, one task is 2 points. Repeat the runs or enlarge the set before declaring a winner.
A claims agent made 200 runs with 150 successes, and total spend was $30. What is the cost per successful task?
Divide spend by successes, not runs: $30 ÷ 150 = $0.20.
In a sandbox run, the agent books the right hotel but charges the customer’s card twice. How should the checker score the run?
Fail: the correct end state includes exactly one charge
Ignore it: sandbox charges are not real
The end state is everything that changed. A double charge is a failed task.
When should the full golden-set eval run for a tutoring agent? Select all that apply.
On every prompt, model or tool change before release
On a schedule, to catch drift
When the provider updates the model version
Anything that changes behaviour, including silent provider updates, should trigger the eval.
After launch, which production signal best stands in for system-level success on a support agent?
The ticket is not reopened within 7 days
Number of messages in the chat
Reopen rate tracks whether the problem was actually solved. Thumbs-up ratings are sparse and biased.
A new model scores 3 points higher on your golden set, but p95 latency goes from 6 s to 14 s. The gate is 8 s. What is the decision?
Block the release: every gate condition must pass
A gate is several conditions, and all must pass. Tune the setup or route traffic before shipping.
process: A reconciliation agent issued the correct refund but called get_account three times. Which technique flags this?
The outcome is fine, but the path is wasteful. Step efficiency catches it.
Reference path: [find_order, get_account, issue_refund]. Actual: [find_order, lookup_fx, get_account, issue_refund]. Which matches pass?
The extra lookup_fx breaks exact match, but the reference steps still appear in order.
Reference: [check_stock, reserve_item, send_confirmation]. Actual: [reserve_item, check_stock, send_confirmation]. Which match passes?
All steps are present, but not in order, so only any-order passes. Reserving before checking stock is a real bug.
What should each trace span record so steps can be scored? Select all that apply.
Name, arguments and result are what you score. Never log secrets or card numbers.
A plan-change task needs 4 steps. The agent took 10. What is the step efficiency?
The agent keeps calling the same lookup tool again and again. Which are likely causes? Select all that apply.
The tool result is missing information the agent needs
All three leave the agent re-checking. Temperature is rarely the root cause; fix the tool description, the result and the stop condition first.
A legal-research agent can reach a good memo by many different search paths. What is the best way to score its steps?
Exact match to one reference path
A per-step rubric scored by an LLM judge
A rubric judges whether each step was sensible without demanding one fixed path.
A transfer agent must complete a KYC check before moving money. Which check enforces this?
A precedence check: check_kyc must come before any transfer call
Order matters here. A plain in-order match would still pass [transfer, check_kyc, transfer], so check that no transfer happens before KYC.
Step scores look perfect, but claims tasks still fail. What is the likely explanation?
The step checks miss what the outcome needs, so run system-level eval too
Good steps do not guarantee a good outcome. Use both levels.
Your team needs to capture agent traces for step scoring. Which tools fit? Select all that apply.
BM25 is a keyword-ranking function, not a tracing tool.
In 6% of runs, issue_refund is called with cur="USD" for an INR account. The outcome check still reads “refund issued”. What catches this?
An argument check on that step: currency must match the account
Argument-level checks catch wrong inputs that a status-only outcome check misses.
In 80 failed traces, 70% of the argument errors come from one tool whose description is ambiguous. What is the best first fix?
Rewrite that tool’s description and parameter schema, then re-run
Clustered errors point to the tool interface. Fix it before touching the model.
A claims agent must never call submit_claim before get_eligibility. How should a violation count?
As a hard fail, even if the final outcome looks right
Ignore it if the claim went through
Only when step efficiency is low
Safety or compliance ordering rules are pass/fail. A good outcome does not excuse them.
A shopping agent calls search_products 25 times until it hits the step limit. Which check flags it?
Loop detection and step efficiency flag this. The fix is usually a clear stop condition.
Which are useful argument-level checks for file_claim? Select all that apply.
claim_id matches the one in the customer’s message
amount is within the policy limit
The argument JSON is neatly indented
Check that arguments are correct for this customer and policy. Formatting does not matter.
You collect 20,000 agent traces a day. How do you apply process-level eval affordably?
Have an LLM judge score every trace
Run cheap code checks on all traces and send a sample to an LLM rubric
Review traces only when customers complain
Code checks scale to every trace. Spend judge calls on a sample and on flagged traces.
An incident agent must read logs before restarting a service. It restarted first, then read the logs, and the incident was resolved. How should this be scored?
Flag it: the required order was broken, even though the outcome was fine
Pass, with a note for the user
Next time, restarting blind could destroy evidence or worsen an outage. Process rules exist for exactly this.
Exact-path match fails on 60% of runs while 90% of outcomes pass. What is the most likely reason?
Exact match is too strict because several paths are valid; use in-order match or a rubric
Exact match only suits tasks with one right path.
Success rate dropped from 91% to 84% after a tool update. What is the fastest way to find out why?
Group the failed traces by their first failing step
Grouping by first failing step points straight at what broke.
A fare-search tool returns “rate_limited”, and the agent retries immediately eight times before it succeeds. What should process eval report?
Retries without backoff, counted as redundant steps and poor error handling
Error handling is part of the path. Immediate retries waste cost and can worsen rate limits.
llmjudge: For weekly claim emails, which check should go to an LLM judge rather than code?
The payout equals the ledger value
The tone is empathetic and the next steps are clear
The email contains the claim ID
Use code for exact facts and a judge for open-ended qualities like tone and clarity.
Which are well-documented LLM-judge biases? Select all that apply.
Position, verbosity and self-preference biases are well documented.
Comparing two product-description generators, the judge prefers whichever answer it reads first. What is the fix?
Judge both orders and count a win only if they agree
If the winner changes with the order, it is not a real preference.
Which scoring scale gives the most consistent judge scores for complaint replies?
Pass/fail or 3 points, with an example for each score
Coarse scales anchored with examples are more repeatable.
The judge and teachers agree 80% of the time on a set where 80% of answers are good. What is the concern?
A judge that always says “good” would also get 80%, so check Cohen’s κ
Add more examples to the rubric
Percent agreement ignores chance. κ corrects for it.
Which are good rubric practices for grading claim summaries? Select all that apply.
Stating that length earns no credit
Vague instructions produce vague, biased scores.
You are grading outputs from Model X. Which judge should you use?
A strong model from a different family
A different model family reduces self-preference bias.
Why ask the judge for its reasoning before the score?
It makes scores more considered and gives a trail to audit
Reasoning first improves scores and leaves something a person can review.
The judge model is upgraded and scores rise 6 points overnight. What should you do?
Re-calibrate the new judge on the human-labelled set before comparing
A new judge is a new ruler. Check it against people first.
The judge gives long support replies higher scores even when the extra text adds nothing. What is happening, and what helps?
Verbosity bias; say in the rubric that length earns nothing and compare against a reference
Judges tend to reward length. Tell the judge explicitly that length earns no credit.
The judge rates confident but medically wrong answers highly. What is the best fix?
Give the judge a vetted reference answer and route high-risk topics to clinician review
Judges can be fooled by fluent answers. Reference-guided grading plus expert review guards high-stakes content.
Which calibration set is best before trusting a judge on contract Q&A?
About 200 real outputs labelled by two domain experts, including failures
20 outputs labelled by the prompt engineer
Calibrate on real, expert-labelled data that includes the failures you care about.
Agreement between the judge and human reviewers is κ = 0.25. Should you trust the judge?
No: agreement is weak; tighten the rubric and add examples, then measure again
Yes, if the judge is a large model
κ around 0.2–0.4 is only fair agreement. Improve the rubric before relying on the judge.
What temperature should a judge run at?
0 or very low, for repeatable scores
As high as possible, to reduce bias
You want the same input to get the same score.
The judge’s scores are stable week to week, but disagreement with the human spot-check has risen from 10% to 25%. What should you do?
Trust the judge: it is stable
Re-calibrate: the product or the answer mix has drifted from what the rubric was tuned on
The weekly human sample exists to catch exactly this drift.
You must choose between two prompt versions for tutoring answers. Which judging set-up fits best?
Pairwise comparison, judged in both orders
One absolute score from a single run
Asking the tutor model which it prefers
Pairwise judging is sensitive to small differences. Swapping the order controls position bias.
Which rubric criteria are concrete enough for a judge? Select all that apply.
States the payout amount exactly as in the claim record
States the next step and its date
Criteria must be checkable. “Good” and “nice” mean different things to different graders.
Each week, 2,000 emails are judged at $0.01 each, and 100 are also reviewed by people at $0.50 each. What is the weekly cost?
The judge must return JSON {score, reason}, but 3% of its replies cannot be parsed. What is the right handling?
Use structured output or validate and retry, and track parse failures separately
Parse failures are an eval-infrastructure bug. They should not quietly shift the scores.
Your judge and your generator are the same model, and judge scores run 8 points above human ratings. What is the likely cause?
Self-preference; use a judge from a different family and re-calibrate
Models tend to rate their own style highly.
agentjudge: When is Agent-as-a-Judge the right choice?
Grading the tone of a chat reply
Verifying a generated codebase meets its spec
It suits work that has to be run or inspected to be verified.
What should a judge agent’s sandbox have? Select all that apply.
Isolate the judge. Never give it production credentials.
The coding agent’s summary says every requirement is met. Why not trust it?
The agent may overstate, so verify with evidence
A self-report is not evidence. Checking the work is.
R1 fails. R2 depends on R1 and looks fine. What is the dependency-aware verdict for R2?
R2 cannot count while its prerequisite fails.
What counts as good evidence for a verdict? Select all that apply.
The file path and lines checked
Evidence is something a person can check for themselves.
What is the main downside of Agent-as-a-Judge compared with LLM-as-a-Judge?
It is slower and costs more per evaluation
Running and inspecting work takes more time and tokens.
There are 4 independent requirements: 3 verified, 1 failed. What is the score?
You want a public set of AI-development tasks with requirement lists to test your judge agent. Which fits?
DevAI came with the Agent-as-a-Judge paper: 55 tasks with 365 requirements.
Where is Agent-as-a-Judge useful? Select all that apply.
Research reports checked against a requirement list
Single-word labels do not need a judge that acts.
How do you make sure the judge agent itself is right?
Spot-check a sample of its verdicts against human review
Audit a sample of verdicts regularly.
A requirement says “drops rows with missing dates”. What should the judge agent do?
Run the pipeline on sample data with missing dates and inspect the output
Test the behaviour with an input that exercises the requirement.
The judge marks “every figure cites a source” as passed, with evidence “the report looks well sourced”. What do you do?
Reject the verdict: evidence must name specific figures and their citations
Evidence has to be specific enough that a reviewer can confirm it quickly.
The judge agent had write access and “fixed” a failing test before judging. What is the problem?
None: the code is better now
The verdict is invalid; judges must be read-only so they measure rather than change the work
It should have fixed more tests
A judge that edits the work is no longer judging it.
A judge agent takes 6 minutes and $0.40 per project, and you get 500 pull requests a day. What is a sensible strategy?
Judge every PR with the agent
Run cheap code checks on every PR and the judge agent on risky changes or a nightly sample
Layer your checks: cheap and broad first, expensive and deep where it matters.
The judge agent ran out of steps before finishing requirement R3. What verdict keeps the judge’s own timeout from being charged to the coding agent?
No evidence means no verdict. Do not count a timeout as a pass or a fail.
Requirement: “the checkout button is disabled when the cart is empty”. What is the best evidence?
Open the page in a headless browser with an empty cart and check the button’s state
Observe the real behaviour in a running app.
Judge verdicts disagree with people on 20% of “performance” requirements such as “should be fast”. What is the fix?
Make the requirement measurable, e.g. “runs in under 60 s on 1M rows”
Vague requirements give inconsistent verdicts. Make them testable.
A contract generator must include 9 mandatory clauses in a 40-page document. Which approach fits best?
A single yes/no from an LLM judge
A judge agent that searches the document and gives a verdict per clause with its location
A verdict per requirement, with a location as evidence, is quick for a person to verify.
Why should the judge agent’s sandbox have no network access?
To stop data leaking and outside content influencing verdicts, and to keep runs reproducible
Isolation protects sensitive data and keeps results repeatable.
What makes requirements easy for a judge to check? Select all that apply.
Vague requirements cannot be verified by anyone, human or agent.
rag: A policy-bot answer makes 5 claims, and 3 are supported by the retrieved chunks. What is the faithfulness?
Faithfulness is 0.93 but context recall is 0.62. What do you fix first?
The model sticks to what it retrieves; it just is not retrieving the right material.
Which metric needs a reference answer?
Recall compares the retrieved context with the facts in the reference answer.
Which are symptoms of a retrieval problem? Select all that apply.
The answer invents a fee no document mentions
An invented fee is a generation problem (faithfulness), not retrieval.
5 chunks are retrieved and 2 are relevant. What share of the retrieved chunks is relevant (unweighted precision@5)?
2 ÷ 5 = 0.4. Ragas’s context precision also weights by rank, so the same 2 chunks score higher when they come first.
The bot says “instant transfer under INR 2 lakh”, but no retrieved chunk says that. What is it?
An unsupported claim is a faithfulness failure.
What are common fixes for low context recall? Select all that apply.
Re-ranking a wider set of candidates
An answer is perfectly faithful to its sources but still wrong. What is the most likely cause?
The retrieved circular was outdated or superseded
Faithfulness only checks against the context. A stale source gives a faithful but wrong answer.
You have no reference answers yet. Which set of checks works without them?
Context relevance, groundedness, answer relevance (the RAG triad)
The RAG triad, popularized by TruLens, needs only the question, the context and the answer.
You need faithfulness and context recall in CI for a Python RAG app this week. Which library fits?
Ragas provides faithfulness, context precision and recall, and more.
A guideline assistant adds dosage advice that is not in the retrieved guideline. How should eval treat it?
Fine, if the advice is correct
As a faithfulness failure that blocks release for high-risk content
In high-stakes domains, anything unsupported by the source is a failure, even if it happens to be true.
An answer cites clause 7.2, but the claim actually comes from clause 9.1, which was also retrieved. What failed?
Citation accuracy; check each claim against the chunk it cites
Users trust citations. Check that each claim is supported by the chunk it points to.
Someone asks about the return window, and all 5 retrieved chunks are about shipping. What does this show?
A retrieval problem: low precision and low recall
Retrieval brought back none of the right material, so the answer cannot be grounded.
Precision is 0.9, recall 0.9 and faithfulness 0.95, but users say answers don’t address their question. Which metric is likely low?
An answer can be grounded yet off-target. Answer relevancy measures whether it addresses the question.
Smaller chunks raised recall from 0.62 to 0.78, but precision dropped. What next?
Add a re-ranker to restore precision while keeping the higher recall
Retrieve more, then re-rank so the best chunks come first.
You are building an eval set for a staff policy assistant. What should it include? Select all that apply.
Reference answers written by compliance experts
Questions the corpus cannot answer, where the bot should decline
Only questions the bot already answers well
Include hard and unanswerable cases, not just the ones that already work.
A question cannot be answered from the policy corpus, and the bot answers from general knowledge. What should eval reward?
Saying it cannot find this in the policy and pointing to a person
For grounded assistants, declining is the correct behaviour when the source is silent.
Your faithfulness score comes from an LLM judge. How do you know you can trust it?
Calibrate it against human-labelled claims on a sample
Judge-based metrics need the same calibration as any LLM judge.
Which metrics can you compute on live traffic with no reference answers? Select all that apply.
Context recall needs a reference answer, so it runs offline on your labelled set.
You can afford reference answers for only 50 questions. Which metric gains most from them?
The others can run without references; context recall cannot.
bench: A vendor says their agent scores 65% on SWE-bench. What do you ask first?
Which split (Full, Lite or Verified), with which harness and scaffold, at what cost
Whether the model is open source
Scores are only comparable on the same split and set-up, and cost matters too.
A patch fixes the issue but breaks another test. Does it count as resolved?
No: the PASS_TO_PASS tests must still pass
Only if the test is flaky
Resolved means the issue is fixed and nothing else broke.
What are the limits of public benchmarks? Select all that apply.
They do not reflect your domain
They are useful for shortlisting, but they do not decide for your use case.
Model B resolves 50% of tasks at $0.10 per attempt. What is its cost per resolved task?
You are shortlisting models for an airline customer-service agent that uses tools and follows policy. Which benchmark fits best?
τ-bench simulates customers in retail and airline domains with tools and policies.
Which benchmark fits a browser agent for e-commerce back-office work?
WebArena hosts realistic websites, including shopping and admin sites.
The public scoreboard favours Model X, but your own 60 internal issues favour Model Y. Which do you choose?
Y, if the internal set reflects your real work
Your own tasks predict your results better.
What should you report alongside a benchmark score? Select all that apply.
Without these, scores cannot be compared fairly.
Before building a tool-heavy trading assistant, you want to shortlist models on function-call accuracy. Which benchmark fits?
You are automating desktop back-office tasks across real apps. Which benchmark fits?
OSWorld tests agents operating real desktop applications.
Your research assistant browses the web, reads files and reasons over many steps. Which benchmark fits?
GAIA targets general assistants with browsing, files and multi-step reasoning.
A model scores 20 points higher on an old benchmark than on a similar one released after its training cutoff. What is the likely cause?
Contamination: old items may have been in its training data
Test items that appear in training data inflate scores.
The top 10 models are all within 1.5 points of each other on a benchmark. What does that mean?
The benchmark is saturated and no longer separates models
All models are equal for your use
Use harder or private evals to tell the models apart.
10,000 tasks a month. Model A resolves 60% at $0.30 per attempt; Model B resolves 50% at $0.10. Unresolved tasks go to people at $2 each. Which is cheaper per month?
A: $3,000 + 4,000 × $2 = $11,000. B: $1,000 + 5,000 × $2 = $11,000. Include the human fallback in the cost.
A model scores pass^1 = 0.61 and pass^8 = 0.25 on τ-bench retail. What does that tell you?
Many tasks succeed only some of the time, so reliability drops sharply over repeated tries
τ-bench introduced pass^k to expose exactly this inconsistency.
You are building a private benchmark from your own repositories. What should you do? Select all that apply.
Hold back a set you never tune prompts on
Include tests that decide pass or fail
Keep it real, held out and automatically checkable.
The same model scores 33% with your in-house agent and 49% on the public board. What is the likely reason?
Differences in scaffold and harness: public entries use tuned agent set-ups
A score belongs to the whole system, not just the model.
Running your 500-issue suite nightly is getting expensive. What is the best move?
Use batch processing and run a small smoke subset on each change
Batch APIs cost about half, and a smoke subset keeps quick feedback on each change.
Your team wants to claim “we beat Model X on SWE-bench”. What makes the claim fair? Select all that apply.
The same split and the official harness
Stating attempts per issue (pass@1 or best of n)
Quietly picking the best of five runs
Be transparent about attempts and set-up. Silent cherry-picking inflates the score.
evaldata: A claims assistant scores 94% on 50 questions an LLM generated from the FAQ, but 85% when sampled real conversations are graded. Which number should the release decision use?
85%: it reflects the traffic the assistant actually sees
Generated questions tend to be easier and tidier than real ones. The score that predicts production is the one measured on production-like cases.
A card-dispute assistant is 90% accurate on 400 test cases. What is the approximate 95% margin?
Where should cases for a claims assistant’s test set come from? Select all that apply.
A redacted sample of production conversations
Support tickets and complaints about the assistant
Cases claims officers say are tricky or high-risk
Only questions the team wrote while building the prompt
Real traffic, complaints and expert knowledge each surface different failures. Questions written by the builders mirror what the prompt already handles.
A UPI help assistant’s fraud-report intent is 0.5% of traffic. With 200 cases sampled purely in proportion, how many fraud reports land in the set, and what should you do?
About 1; set a floor per stratum so it gets at least a few cases
None; fraud cases cannot be tested
0.5% of 200 is 1 case, too few to score. A floor per stratum keeps rare but costly intents in the set; reweight when reporting the overall score.
Two nurses label triage answers. They agree on 90% of cases, and each marks 90% of cases as pass. What is Cohen’s κ, roughly?
Chance agreement = 0.9² + 0.1² = 0.82. κ = (0.90 − 0.82) ÷ (1 − 0.82) = 0.08 ÷ 0.18 ≈ 0.44: moderate, much weaker than 90% suggests.
A plan-change assistant moves from 82% to 85% on a 100-case test set. What can you conclude?
Not much: each score has a margin of about ±7 points
It is worse, because the set is small
1.96 × √(0.85 × 0.15 ÷ 100) ≈ 0.07, so about ±7 points on each score. A 3-point change is well inside the noise.
Which are signs that a returns assistant has been overfitted to its test set? Select all that apply.
The test score rose 8 points over a month of prompt tweaks, but complaints did not fall
The prompt now contains phrases copied from specific test cases
A holdout nobody tuned on scores far lower than the main set
Scores on the main set and the holdout are within a point of each other
Gains that do not carry to a holdout or to users, and prompts that quote test cases, are classic overfitting. Matching holdout scores are a good sign.
Labels are wrong 10% of the time, at random. The new release is truly 5 points worse. Roughly what drop will the test set show?
With symmetric label noise e, a real difference shrinks by (1 − 2e) = 1 − 0.2 = 0.8, so 5 × 0.8 = 4 points. Noisy labels hide real changes.
An NBFC’s loan-query assistant is about 80% accurate. How many cases give a 95% margin of ±2.5 points?
A bank has only 2 real conversations about locker nominations. How should synthetic cases be used?
Replace the whole test set with synthetic cases
Generate a few for that stratum and keep only those a subject expert approves
Generate hundreds so the stratum dominates the score
Synthetic cases are useful gap-fillers when reviewed. They should not replace real traffic or distort the overall score.
Before annotators read production conversations from a hospital’s billing assistant, which fields should be redacted? Select all that apply.
The detected intent, such as “bill dispute”
Diagnosis details not needed to judge the answer
Remove personal and health details that labelling does not need, in line with DPDP expectations. The intent is what annotators are judging.
A wallet’s Hindi slice has 60 test cases and scores 80%. What is its 95% margin?
1.96 × √(0.8 × 0.2 ÷ 60) = 1.96 × 0.0516 ≈ 0.101, about ±10.1 points. Slice scores need far more cases than the overall score suggests.
A customer reports that the assistant told her a flood claim needs a police report, which is wrong. After the prompt is fixed, what should happen to the case?
Label it and add it to the next test-set version, so the regression is caught if it returns
Add it to the prompt as an example only
Every production failure is a test case you know matters. Adding it, redacted and labelled, stops the same mistake returning unnoticed.
Why keep a holdout slice of the test set that nobody looks at while tuning prompts?
To check that improvements carry over to cases the team did not tune against
Holdouts are only needed for fine-tuning
Repeated tuning against the same cases overfits them. The untouched holdout shows whether a gain is real.
Which are useful adversarial cases for a claims assistant? Select all that apply.
A claim PDF with hidden text telling the assistant to approve the claim
A claim number that does not exist
A routine “what is my motor claim status?” question
Adversarial cases probe injection, invented facts and hostile users. A routine status query belongs in the ordinary stratified sample.
A test set of 150 cases gives a margin of about ±6 points. How many cases would give about ±3 points at the same accuracy?
The margin shrinks with √n, so halving it needs four times the cases: 150 × 4 = 600.
Two teams report 88% and 91% for the same assistant, but neither names the test-set version. What is the problem?
The numbers cannot be compared, because the sets may differ
The lower score must be wrong
Only the higher score should be published
A score means something only with the dataset version it came from. Version the set and log it with every result.
Two annotators disagree on 15% of discharge-summary cases. What is the best next step?
Have a senior clinician adjudicate each disagreement and clarify the rubric where it caused them
Drop all disputed cases from the set
Adjudication fixes the gold labels, and rewriting unclear rubric lines stops the same disagreements next time. Dropping disputed cases removes the hardest ones.
A set of 1,000 synthetic English cases reports 94% ± 1.5 points, yet misses a real regression in Hindi answers. Why?
The set is precise about the wrong questions: it has no Hindi cases
A narrow margin only means the estimate is stable for the cases in the set. If a slice is missing, no amount of precision will reveal failures there.
A stratified set is 75% English and 25% Hindi, but traffic is 80% English and 20% Hindi. English accuracy is 90% and Hindi 70%. What overall accuracy should you report for traffic?
Reweight to the traffic mix: 0.8 × 90% + 0.2 × 70% = 72% + 14% = 86%. The unweighted set average, 0.75 × 90% + 0.25 × 70% = 85%, understates it.
usersim: What does a user simulator do?
Plays the user in a multi-turn conversation
Why do scripted user turns overstate quality?
They never react to what the agent says
An agent that skips a question still passes.
What belongs on a scenario card? Select all that apply.
Hidden details and when to reveal them
An agent succeeds 80% of the time per run. pass^2?
The simulator pastes the account number in its first message. Problem?
The agent never has to ask, so the test is too easy
Which personas make simulation realistic for Indian users? Select all that apply.
The LLM user breaking character or leaking hidden details
Scripted tests report 95%; real users 71%. Gap?
Why run each scenario more than once?
Both agent and simulator are stochastic, so reliability needs repeats
Which benchmark popularised pass^k for tool-agent-user tasks?
What stops a conversation in the harness?
The simulator says DONE or a turn limit is reached
Which are limits of user simulation? Select all that apply.
Simulated users are not real users
The agent says “refund initiated” but raises no ticket. Result?
Where do good scenario cards come from?
Which technique covers building the scenario set itself?
An agent at 90% per run. pass^3?
After launch, simulation should be complemented by?
Keep real users in the loop.
pairwise: What does a pairwise judge decide?
Which of two answers to the same question is better
Why judge each pair in both orders?
B wins 400, loses 304, ties 96 of 800. Win rate with ties as half?
The 95% interval is 49% to 63%. What can you conclude?
The data cannot tell them apart yet
To halve the interval width you need about?
Which practices make a comparison trustworthy? Select all that apply.
Fixing the question set in advance
Stopping as soon as B is ahead
The judge always sees B second and favours slot 1. Effect?
B’s gain is hidden or reversed
800 pairs judged in both orders at ₹0.60 a call cost?
Which test fits paired win/loss counts with ties removed?
How are many versions ranked from pairwise votes?
Why are paired comparisons more precise than two separate averages?
Each question is its own control.
A judge splits on 30% of pairs. What does that suggest?
The judge or rubric is inconsistent
Which belong in an eval report for a ship decision? Select all that apply.
A 0.3-point gain on a 10-point scale over 50 questions is?
Likely within noise; needs an interval
Which technique covers writing the judge’s rubric?
This one covers comparing and deciding.
Minimum gain worth shipping is 5 points; current win-rate interval is ±7. What next?
Make the interval narrower than the gain.
Which are common LLM judge biases? Select all that apply.
Win rate 46% with B always second, 56% with both orders. The difference comes from?

system.q: In your own words: why can a 94% success rate from a single run give a false picture for an agent?
pts: one run can pass by luck
system.model: Agents don’t produce the same result every time. A single run can pass by luck, so 94% may hide tasks that only work sometimes. Running each task several times and reporting pass^k shows how many tasks work every time, which is what customers actually experience.

system.q: How would you design a release gate for a customer-support agent?
pts: a golden set of real tasks
cost and latency, not just quality
system.model: Build a versioned golden set of 50–200 real, anonymized tasks including past failures, each with an end state code can check. Run each 3–5 times. Gate on success rate and pass^k above set thresholds, plus cost per success and p95 latency limits, so a release that is slower or pricier is blocked even when quality holds.

system.q: What does system-level eval miss, and what would you pair it with?
system.model: It only sees the outcome, so it can’t say why a run failed or catch harmful intermediate actions, such as a wrong-currency refund that was later corrected. Pair it with process-level eval on traces to find the failing step.

process.q: Explain exact, in-order and any-order trajectory matching with an example.
process.model: Exact match requires the same tool sequence with nothing extra. In-order match requires the reference steps in the right order but allows extra steps. Any-order match only requires each reference step somewhere. For reference [find_order, get_account, refund], the trace [find_order, get_account, get_account, refund] fails exact but passes in-order and any-order.

process.q: An agent’s refunds succeed, but it costs 3× more than expected. How do you investigate?
process.model: Pull the traces for those runs and score each step: step efficiency, redundant calls and loops. Aggregate by tool to see where the waste concentrates. The usual root causes are a vague tool description, a tool result missing information the agent then re-fetches, or no clear stop condition.

process.q: Why do argument checks matter even when the task “succeeds”?
pts: wrong values have real side effects
process.model: A run can reach a “refund issued” state while the amount or currency was wrong, so outcome checks pass while customers are harmed. Argument checks catch these silent errors, which matter most for money, compliance and safety.

llmjudge.q: How would you build a trustworthy LLM judge for claim summaries?
pts: temperature 0 or a different model family
llmjudge.model: Write a pass/fail rubric with concrete criteria and an example of each outcome. Use a strong model from a different family at temperature 0, ask for reasoning before the score, and parse only the final score. Hand-label 50–100 summaries and check agreement and Cohen’s κ before trusting it, then re-check regularly.

llmjudge.q: Name the main judge biases and how you counter each.
pts: verbosity bias → rubric says length earns nothing
self-preference → use a different model family
llmjudge.model: Position bias: judge both orders and count only consistent wins. Verbosity bias: state in the rubric that length earns nothing. Self-preference: use a judge from a different model family than the one being graded.

llmjudge.q: Why isn’t 80% agreement with humans always good enough?
pts: look deeper: per category or confusion matrix
llmjudge.model: If 80% of answers are good, a judge that always says “good” also agrees 80% of the time. Cohen’s κ corrects for chance agreement. Also check agreement per category and look at the confusion matrix to see which errors the judge makes.

agentjudge.q: When would you use Agent-as-a-Judge instead of LLM-as-a-Judge?
pts: the judge must act: run or inspect
agentjudge.model: When correctness can only be confirmed by acting on the work: running code, opening files, checking outputs. That fits long, artifact-producing tasks such as codebases or data pipelines, and it gives verdicts backed by evidence rather than a reading of the text.

agentjudge.q: How do you keep a judge agent safe?
agentjudge.model: Run it in an isolated sandbox with the work mounted read-only, no network access, no production credentials, and time and step limits. Require evidence for each verdict and spot-check verdicts against human review.

It counts a requirement only if everything it depends on also passed. A step that looks fine but builds on a failed prerequisite is marked blocked, so the score reflects working software rather than disconnected pieces.

rag.q: Explain faithfulness and context recall, and how they differ.
pts: recall: reference facts found in context
one diagnoses generation, the other retrieval
rag.model: Faithfulness is the share of the answer’s claims supported by the retrieved context: it checks generation. Context recall is the share of the reference answer’s facts that appear in the retrieved context: it checks retrieval. Together they tell you which half to fix.

rag.q: Your bot invented a fee. Walk through your diagnosis.
pts: which half|retrieval or generation|generation or retrieval|fix
a fix such as a grounding check
rag.model: Split the answer into claims and check each against the retrieved chunks: the fee claim will be unsupported, lowering faithfulness. Then check context recall to see whether the correct fee information was retrieved at all. If it was, fix generation with a grounding check or prompt change; if not, fix retrieval first.

rag.q: Why can a perfectly faithful answer still be wrong?
pts: the source is wrong or outdated
faithfulness only compares with the context
rag.model: Faithfulness only checks that the answer matches the retrieved context. If that document is wrong or outdated, the answer is faithfully wrong. Keeping the knowledge base current and curated matters as much as the metrics.

bench.q: What does SWE-bench Verified measure, and how?
bench.model: Whether an agent can resolve real GitHub issues from Python repositories. The agent writes a patch; the harness applies it in a Docker environment and runs the tests. It counts as resolved only if the FAIL_TO_PASS tests now pass and the PASS_TO_PASS tests still pass. Verified is a 500-issue subset checked by human annotators.

bench.q: Why shouldn’t a scoreboard alone decide which model you ship?
bench.model: Benchmark items may have leaked into training data, top scores bunch together, and public tasks rarely look like your domain or constraints. Use the scoreboard to shortlist, then decide with a private eval on your own tasks, including cost per resolved task.

bench.q: Model A resolves 62% at $0.40 per task; B resolves 58% at $0.10. Which would you pick, and why?
pts: B is much cheaper per success
bench.model: Compare cost per resolved task: A is $0.40 ÷ 0.62 ≈ $0.65, B is $0.10 ÷ 0.58 ≈ $0.17. B is about 4× cheaper per success for 4 points less, so it’s usually the better pick, as long as both are confirmed on your own tasks.

evaldata.q: Explain how you would build and maintain the evaluation dataset for an insurance claims assistant.
evaldata.model: Sample real conversations, tickets and cases claims officers flag, after redacting personal data. Stratify by intent, language and risk with a floor per stratum, and add adversarial cases and expert-reviewed synthetic ones where real cases are thin. Label against a written rubric with two annotators, measure agreement with Cohen’s κ and adjudicate disagreements. Size the set for the margin you need, version it, keep a holdout nobody tunes on, and add new production failures every cycle.

evaldata.q: The assistant is about 85% accurate. How many cases give a 95% margin of ±2 points, and roughly how many to reliably see a 4-point change between two versions? Show the working.
evaldata.model: For one score: n = 3.8416 × 0.85 × 0.15 ÷ 0.02² = 0.4898 ÷ 0.0004 ≈ 1,225 cases.
