To see a 4-point change between two versions, the margin on the difference is about √2 times the single-score margin, so it must be under 4 points: each score needs a margin under about 2.8 points, which is n ≈ 0.4898 ÷ 0.0283² ≈ 612 in theory. Label noise shrinks the measured change and real sets have slices to cover, so about 900 to 1,000 cases is a safer size. Paired comparisons on the same cases are tighter still.

evaldata.q: The team’s test set scores 94%, yet complaints from Hindi-speaking customers are rising and a new flood-claim intent keeps failing. Diagnose the dataset.
pts: fix: stratify and refresh from failures
evaldata.model: A 94% score on a set that does not look like traffic says little. It was likely generated or hand-written in English, so it has no Hindi slice, and it predates the flood-claim intent, so the failures that matter are absent. Rebuild it from stratified production samples with a Hindi quota and a floor per intent, label it with two annotators, report per-slice scores with margins, and add each month’s new failures to the next version.

usersim.q: How would you evaluate a multi-turn support agent before launch?
usersim.model: Write scenario cards from real conversations with a persona, goal, hidden details and expected end state. An LLM plays the user under rules to stay in character and reveal details only when asked. Check the backend end state, run each scenario k times and report pass^1 and pass^k by persona.

usersim.q: The agent passes 95% of tests but real users succeed 71% of the time. Why, and what do you change?
usersim.model: Scripted turns never react to the agent, and the personas are too easy. Switch to LLM-simulated users with scenario cards, weight personas like real users (Hinglish, impatient, withholding), and score by the backend end state.

pairwise.q: How would you decide whether to ship a new prompt?
pairwise.model: Fix a question set and the smallest gain worth shipping, answer every question with both versions, judge each pair in both orders with splits as ties, and ship only if the 95% interval of the win rate is above 50%.

pairwise.q: A teammate reports B scored 7.9 against A’s 7.6 on 50 questions and wants to ship. Your reply?
pairwise.model: A 0.3 difference on 50 questions is within noise. Compare pairwise on the same questions in both orders, report the win rate with a 95% interval, and use enough questions that the interval can clear 50%.

cases.title: Your KYC agent passed QA, but complaints doubled
cases.brief: A brokerage launched an agent that verifies new customers’ KYC documents and answers their questions from the internal policy manual. It passed a 50-case QA suite at 94%. Two weeks after launch, complaints have doubled. Management wants an evaluation plan before the next release.
evidence: The QA suite has 50 cases, each run once, and every case was written by the team from memory before launch: 94% success.
Of the complaints, 38% say they were given a rejection reason that is not in the policy manual, and 8% report an account approved with mismatched PAN details.
27% say verification was slow. Traces of every run are stored, and some show fifteen or more tool calls for one verification, but nobody reviews them.
Part of the team wants to switch to the model that tops a public scoreboard, on the strength of its score.
cases.task: Choose the techniques you would apply, put them in order, and say which symptom each one fixes. The headline number is the first thing to doubt.

why.evaldata: Start here, because every other number depends on it. Fifty cases written from memory, each run once, is not a test set — it is a rehearsal. Rebuild it from real traffic and real complaints, cover every slice that reaches production, have two people label the hard ones, and size each slice so a four-point drop cannot hide inside the margin. Until this is fixed, 94% is not a measurement of anything.
why.system: With a trustworthy set, score the thing that matters: was the account correctly approved or rejected? Run each case three to five times, because one lucky run hides flakiness, and report pass^k alongside cost and latency. That becomes the release gate the last launch did not have.
why.process: Two symptoms are about the path, not the outcome. Fifteen tool calls for one verification is waste you can only see in a trajectory, and an approval with mismatched PAN details means the step order itself is wrong — did verify_pan run, with the right arguments, before approve_account? The traces are already being stored; start scoring them.
why.rag: A rejection reason that is not in the policy manual is an unsupported claim, which is exactly what faithfulness measures. Score the answer against the retrieved policy sections to catch invented reasons, and measure context recall to find out whether retrieval is missing the right sections in the first place — those are two different bugs with two different fixes.
why.llmjudge: Useful as a second layer once correctness is measured: a judge with a written rubric can grade the clarity and tone of rejection explanations at a scale no human review would reach. Calibrate it against human labels before you trust it, and keep it away from the correctness questions above, which have checkable answers.
why.pairwise: Useful for the decision in the last piece of evidence. If a model switch is on the table, run both on the same rebuilt cases, in both orders, and report a win rate with an interval — ship only if it clears 50% convincingly. That is how you answer “is the new one better” without a scoreboard.
why.agentjudge: Not needed: this agent does not produce a multi-file artifact that has to be inspected or run. The end state — approved or rejected, with the right reason — is checkable directly, so the cost and the extra failure modes of a judge agent buy nothing here.
why.bench: Not the tool for this decision, and the last piece of evidence is a trap. A public scoreboard says nothing about your policy manual or India’s KYC rules, its test items may be in the model’s training data, and its setup is not your production setup. Benchmarks help you shortlist before you build; they never decide a release.
why.usersim: Not needed on this evidence: nothing here points at multi-turn behaviour. The failures are a bad test set, wrong outcomes, wasteful paths and unsupported claims — all of which show up in single exchanges. Worth adding if customers start negotiating with the agent over several turns.

firstWhy.system: Close, and it is the right second step. But running a bad test set more carefully gives you a more precise wrong answer — fifty cases written from memory will not show you the failures that are generating complaints.
firstWhy.process: The traces will tell you a great deal, and two symptoms need them. But you would be debugging without knowing which cases matter, because the set that said 94% does not contain the failing ones.
firstWhy.rag: The invented rejection reasons are the loudest complaint, and faithfulness is the right instrument. Still, you have nothing to run it on until the test set reflects real traffic.
firstWhy.bench: A scoreboard cannot see your policy manual. This is the one piece of evidence that is there to be rejected, not acted on.

cases.firstHint: You have the right techniques. Now ask which one every other number on this page depends on: three of your steps produce scores, and all three are measured on something written from memory.

evaldata: Look again at the first symptom: fifty cases, each run once, written by the team from memory before launch. Before you measure anything, what do you have to be able to trust — and what on this page is about the thing you measure with?

The problem is not how the score was computed, it is what it was computed on. Real traffic instead of recollection, every slice that reaches production, two labellers on the hard ones, and enough cases per slice to see a small drop.
Eval Datasets. Note what it says about synthetic-only sets and about how many cases a slice needs.
system: A single run of each case produced 94%. Complaints say otherwise. What does running the same case several times tell you that running it once cannot, and what should a release gate actually score?
Score the end state rather than the wording — was the account correctly approved or rejected — repeat each case, and report the repeated-trial figure along with cost and latency.
System-Level Eval. Note what pass^k is for, and why a single lucky run is dangerous.
process: Two symptoms are not about the answer at all: fifteen tool calls for one verification, and an approval that went through with mismatched PAN details. A pass or fail on the outcome cannot explain either. What can?
The traces are already stored. Score the path itself: which steps ran, in what order, with what arguments — did the check run before the approval?
Process-Level Eval. Note what it catches that an outcome score cannot, including agents that succeed wastefully.
rag: 38% of complaints describe a rejection reason that is not in the policy manual. The agent answers from that manual. What would you measure to tell an invented reason from a correctly quoted one?
Two different numbers matter here: whether the answer stayed inside the sources it was given, and whether the right sources were retrieved at all. They point to different fixes.
RAG Grounding Metrics. Note the difference between faithfulness and context recall, and which one needs ground-truth answers.

drop.agentjudge: An agent judge earns its cost when the deliverable has to be opened, inspected or executed. What artifact does this agent produce that you would need to run?
drop.bench: A public scoreboard is the fourth piece of evidence, and it is there to be questioned. What does a leaderboard know about your policy manual or your KYC rules?
drop.usersim: Simulated users test what happens over several turns. Which of these four symptoms describes a conversation rather than a single exchange?

whyFirst.q: Before you check — which is the strongest reason for a step to go first in this case?
options: The invented rejection reasons are 38% of complaints, the largest single group, so they should be fixed first.
Every score on this page — the 94%, any judge, any model comparison — is computed on fifty cases written from memory, so none of them means anything yet.
Traces are already being stored, so scoring them costs nothing and is the cheapest place to start.
whyFirst.why: Measurement has a dependency order. A faithfulness score, a release gate and a model comparison are all only as good as the cases they run on, and this set was written from recollection before launch and never refreshed from the failures. Fix what you measure with, and every number after it becomes worth arguing about.

cases.model: Start with the test set, because every other number depends on it: rebuild the fifty remembered cases from real traffic and real complaints, cover every slice that reaches production, double-label the hard ones, and size the slices so a small regression cannot hide in the margin. Then make the gate trustworthy — score the end state rather than the phrasing, run each case three to five times, and report pass^k with cost and latency. With that in place, turn to the two path failures: score the stored traces for the fifteen-call verifications and, more urgently, for whether verify_pan ran with matching details before approve_account. Alongside, measure faithfulness against the policy manual to catch the invented rejection reasons and context recall to see whether retrieval is missing sections at all. Once correctness is measured, a calibrated judge can grade the clarity of explanations, and a paired comparison with both orders can settle any model switch. The public scoreboard decides nothing here, and there is no artifact for an agent judge to run.
cases.note: Fix what you measure with, then what you measure, then where it went wrong. Case 2 looks like the same problem and has a different answer — there the test set is fine and the tests are simply the wrong shape.

cases.title: Green offline, broken in the conversation
cases.brief: A telecom operator’s support agent changes plans, applies credits and answers billing questions over chat. The offline eval suite has 400 real cases, properly labelled and sliced, and scores 91%. Customer satisfaction on chats longer than four turns is the lowest of any channel. The team is about to ship its fourth prompt rewrite this month.
evidence: The eval suite is built from real tickets, split by intent and language, with two labellers on the ambiguous ones. Nobody disputes the set.
Every case in it is a single question with a single expected answer. Production conversations average six turns.
One in five conversations longer than four turns ends with the customer repeating something they already said; the agent asks for the plan name again after confirming it.
Three prompt versions shipped this month. Each was chosen after someone read about twenty outputs and said it looked better. Nobody can say which of the three is best.
The judge used to score reply tone has no written rubric, and its scores have never been compared with a human’s. Longer replies tend to win.
cases.task: Choose the techniques you would apply, put them in order, and say which symptom each one fixes. One piece of evidence is here to rule a technique out rather than to be fixed.

why.usersim: The test set is fine; its shape is wrong. Four hundred single-turn cases cannot find a failure that only appears on turn five, which is precisely where this agent breaks. Put an LLM in the customer’s seat with a goal and a persona, let it react to what the agent actually says, check the end state of the whole conversation rather than each reply, and repeat each scenario to report pass^k. Give it the personas you really get — impatient, Hinglish, holding back detail until asked — not a polite English script.
why.llmjudge: The judge is deciding which prompt ships, and it is unfit for that: no rubric, no calibration, and a visible preference for length. Write the rubric first, make it ask for reasoning before a score, run pairwise comparisons in both orders to cancel position bias, and calibrate against human labels on a sample before trusting any number it produces. A biased judge does not just add noise — it points the whole team in the wrong direction.
why.pairwise: Three versions shipped on twenty eyeballed outputs each is not a decision, it is a mood. Run the candidates on the same scenarios, in both orders, and report a paired win rate with an interval; ship only if it clears 50% convincingly. Compare paired outcomes on identical inputs rather than two separate averages, and stop peeking at the running total.
why.evaldata: Useful, and narrower than it looks: the existing set is genuinely good, so this is not a rebuild. What it needs is the language and persona slices the simulator will exercise, and enough conversations per slice that a real difference clears the margin.
why.system: Useful: once conversations are simulated, each one needs a checkable end state — was the plan actually changed, was the credit actually applied — scored over repeated runs rather than per reply. On its own it changes nothing, because single-turn cases already pass.
why.process: Not needed here, and this is the interesting one to leave out. The agent calls the right tools with the right arguments; nothing in the trajectory is malformed. It loses the thread of the conversation, which is a dialogue-state failure, not a step-order failure. Trace scoring would show you a clean path through a conversation the customer gave up on.
why.rag: Not needed: the answers come from a plan catalogue and the customer’s own account, not from a document corpus. There is no retrieved context to be faithful to, so grounding metrics have nothing to score.
why.agentjudge: Not needed: a chat reply is not an artifact to be inspected or executed. There is no workspace to open.
why.bench: Not needed: no model choice is in question, and no public suite contains your plan catalogue or your six-turn billing conversations.

firstWhy.llmjudge: The judge does need fixing, and soon — it is choosing what ships. But a calibrated judge pointed at single-turn cases still cannot see the turn-five failure, so fix what you are testing before you fix the thing that scores it.
firstWhy.pairwise: Right instrument, wrong moment. A paired comparison on single-turn cases would tell you, with proper error bars, which version is better at something that is not failing.
firstWhy.evaldata: Understandable — it is the habit case 1 teaches. But read the first piece of evidence again: this set is real, sliced and double-labelled. It is not the problem.
firstWhy.system: End-state scoring is part of the answer, but there are no multi-turn runs to score yet. Build the conversations first.

cases.firstHint: The right three techniques. Now ask which of them the other two are measured on: a calibrated judge and a paired comparison both need something to run, and single-turn cases are not it.

usersim: The second and third symptoms describe something that only happens from turn four onwards, and every test case is one question with one answer. What kind of test could ever catch that?
Something has to play the customer — with a goal, a personality, and the freedom to react to whatever the agent just said — and the thing you score is how the whole conversation ended.
User Simulation for Multi-Turn Agents. Note what it says about scripted turns and about which personas you test with.
llmjudge: The last symptom: no rubric, never compared with a human, and longer replies tend to win. Something is already scoring this agent. What has to be true of it before any of its numbers mean anything?
Name the biases it is showing, then fix each one: a written rubric, reasoning before the score, both orders in a pairwise run, and a calibration check against human labels.
LLM-as-a-Judge. Note the three named biases and what each one is fixed with.
pairwise: Three versions shipped this month, each chosen by reading about twenty outputs. What is missing from “it looked better”, and what turns it into a decision you could defend?
Same inputs for every candidate, both presentation orders, and a win rate reported with an interval rather than a single number — and no stopping early because one is ahead.
Pairwise Comparison and Statistical Significance. Note why paired outcomes beat two separate averages.

drop.process: Trace scoring finds a step that ran in the wrong order or with the wrong arguments. Read the third symptom again: is the agent calling the wrong tool, or forgetting something it was already told?
drop.rag: Grounding metrics score an answer against retrieved context. Where would the retrieved context come from in a plan change?
drop.agentjudge: An agent judge opens, inspects and runs the deliverable. What is the deliverable of a billing chat?
drop.bench: Which of these five symptoms is about choosing a model?

whyFirst.q: Before you check — which is the strongest reason for a step to go first in this case?
options: The eval set should be rebuilt, because 91% clearly does not match what customers experience.
The judge is biased towards long replies, and it is deciding which prompt ships, so nothing can be trusted until it is calibrated.
Nothing can be measured about turn five until the tests have a turn five, so the shape of the test has to change before anything that scores it.
whyFirst.why: In case 1 the set itself was untrustworthy and rebuilding it came first. Here the set is real, sliced and double-labelled — and still useless for this failure, because every case stops after one exchange. The gap is not quality, it is shape. Fix that, and the judge and the comparison finally have the right thing to run on.

cases.model: The set is not the problem — the shape of the tests is. Start by simulating the conversation: an LLM in the customer’s seat with a goal and a persona, reacting to what the agent actually says, scored on the end state of the whole exchange and repeated so you can report pass^k, with the impatient and Hinglish personas you really get rather than a polite English script. Then fix the instrument that is choosing what ships: give the judge a written rubric, ask for reasoning before the score, run both orders, and calibrate it against human labels on a sample. Only then does comparing versions mean anything — run the candidates on the same simulated scenarios in both orders and report a paired win rate with an interval, rather than shipping on twenty eyeballed outputs. Add the language and persona slices to the set as you go, and give each simulated conversation a checkable end state. Trace scoring, grounding metrics, an agent judge and public benchmarks all address problems this agent does not have; the trajectory is clean, which is exactly why the trajectory is not where to look.
cases.note: Compare this with case 1. Both are agents that score well and fail in production, and the first move is different in each: there the test set was fiction, here it is real and simply the wrong shape. Ask what your tests cannot see before you ask how to score them better.

cases.title: The migration that passed review and broke production
cases.brief: A bank’s data platform team runs an agent that migrates legacy ETL jobs to a new orchestrator. Each task produces twenty to forty changed files: DAG definitions, SQL, config and tests. Review is a human skimming the diff summary and approving. Last month a migration that passed review took a reporting pipeline down for a day.
evidence: Every unit test the agent writes passes, on every task.
The migration that broke production generated a DAG referencing a table that does not exist in the target warehouse. Nothing in the evaluation ever executed the generated code.
The eval tasks were written from memory by the same engineer who wrote the agent’s prompt, and there are eleven of them.
Scoring is one call to a model with the prompt “is this code good?”, answered on the diff alone. It has never disagreed with a human reviewer, because nobody has checked.
Two coding models are being considered for next quarter, and the team is reading a public leaderboard to decide which to trial.
cases.task: Choose the techniques you would apply, put them in order, and say which symptom each one fixes. One piece of evidence looks reassuring and is not evidence of anything.

why.system: Start with the cheapest thing that would have caught the outage: a checkable end state, actually executed. Stand the generated DAG up against the target warehouse, run it, and score whether it completes and produces the expected rows — not whether the diff reads well. Repeat each task, because a migration that works once and fails on a retry is not migrated, and gate the release on that outcome with its cost and runtime attached.
why.agentjudge: An end-state check tells you the pipeline ran; it does not tell you the work meets the spec. Twenty to forty files per task is exactly the deliverable an agent judge is for: give it the ticket and the workspace, let it open the files, run the queries, check that every legacy job has a counterpart and that config points at the right environment. Keep it isolated so it cannot edit what it is judging, and audit its findings — it makes mistakes too.
why.evaldata: Eleven tasks written from memory by the person who wrote the prompt is the narrowest possible test set, and it is tuned, however unintentionally, to the agent’s strengths. Rebuild it from real migration tickets, including the ones that went badly, cover the job types that actually exist in the estate, and add every production failure to the set as it happens so the same outage cannot pass twice.
why.bench: Useful, and this is the one case on this page where a public benchmark earns its place: the last piece of evidence is a model choice for next quarter, before anything is built. Use leaderboards to shortlist two or three candidates, then decide on your own migration tasks. Read them with contamination and saturation in mind, and never let one settle a release.
why.process: Useful for long-horizon work: a task that touches forty files has a long trajectory, and scoring it shows where a migration went off course — which files it opened, whether it inspected the target schema before writing against it. Worth adding once the outcome is actually being checked, because it explains failures rather than catching them.
why.llmjudge: Not needed, and asking a model “is this code good?” on the diff alone is the practice that already failed. A single judgement from reading code cannot know whether a table exists in the warehouse; that is a question for execution, not opinion. If a judge stays anywhere here, it is inside the agent judge, with a rubric, looking at evidence it gathered by running things.
why.rag: Not needed: the agent writes code against a schema and a ticket, not answers from a document corpus. There is no retrieved context for an answer to be faithful to.
why.usersim: Not needed: there is no conversation. The task arrives as a ticket and the deliverable is a set of files.
why.pairwise: Not needed yet, and the order matters. A paired comparison decides between two candidates once you have a trustworthy gate to compare them on — and right now the gate is one model reading a diff against eleven remembered tasks. Build the gate, then compare.

firstWhy.evaldata: Defensible — eleven remembered tasks is a real problem, and in case 1 the set came first. But here something simpler would have caught the outage: nothing ever ran the generated code. Fix that, and even eleven tasks start catching outages.
firstWhy.agentjudge: The right instrument for a forty-file deliverable, and it is your second step. But an agent judge is slow and expensive, and the specific failure that took production down — a table that does not exist — is caught by executing the pipeline, which is cheaper.
firstWhy.bench: A leaderboard is next quarter’s question. A reporting pipeline was down for a day.
firstWhy.llmjudge: Asking a model to read the diff more carefully is what is already happening. The problem is that reading is not running.

cases.firstHint: The right techniques. Now ask which one would have caught last month’s outage on its own, and which of them are slower and more expensive than that.

system: The DAG referenced a table that does not exist, and nothing in the evaluation ever executed the generated code. Before any judging, what is the checkable end state of a migrated pipeline, and what has to happen to it?
Stand the artifact up in the target environment, run it, and score whether it completed and produced what it should — more than once, in case it only works on the first attempt.
System-Level Eval. Note what a checkable end state is, and why repeated trials matter.
agentjudge: Each task changes twenty to forty files, and the current review is someone skimming a diff summary. Running the pipeline proves it executes. What is still unchecked about whether the work matches the ticket?

Something that does what a careful reviewer would: opens the workspace, reads the files, runs the queries, and checks the deliverable against the requirement — in isolation, so it cannot alter what it is judging.
Agent-as-a-Judge. Note what it inspects beyond the output, and why it needs isolation and auditing.
evaldata: Eleven tasks, written from memory, by the same engineer who wrote the agent’s prompt. What is wrong with that as a measuring instrument — and where should migration tasks come from instead?
Real tickets rather than recollection, the job types that actually exist in the estate, and every production failure folded back in so the same outage cannot pass a second time.
Eval Datasets. Note what it says about overfitting to the same cases and about refreshing from failures.

drop.llmjudge: One model answering “is this code good?” from the diff is the fourth symptom, not the fix. What can execution tell you that reading cannot?
drop.rag: Grounding metrics compare an answer with its retrieved sources. What corpus is this agent answering from?
drop.usersim: Simulated users test multi-turn conversations. How many turns does a migration ticket have?
drop.pairwise: A paired comparison needs a trustworthy gate to compare on. What would you be running the two models against today?

whyFirst.q: Before you check — which is the strongest reason for a step to go first in this case?
options: Nothing in the evaluation has ever executed the generated code, so the cheapest check that would have caught the outage does not exist yet.
Eleven tasks written from memory is the weakest test set on the page, so it should be rebuilt before anything else.
A forty-file deliverable needs a judge that can inspect a whole workspace, which is the only thing capable of reviewing this properly.
whyFirst.why: All three are true, and they are not equally urgent. The outage was a DAG pointing at a table that does not exist — a failure that execution catches immediately and that no amount of reading catches at all. Rebuilding the task set and adding a judge agent both matter, and both are slower and more expensive than running the thing. Start with the check that would have caught the incident.

cases.model: Start by running the work, because nothing ever has: define the checkable end state of a migrated pipeline, stand the generated DAG up against the target warehouse, execute it, and score whether it completes and produces the expected rows — repeated, with cost and runtime reported, as the release gate. Then add an agent judge for everything execution cannot see: give it the ticket and the workspace, let it open files and run queries to confirm every legacy job has a counterpart and config points at the right environment, keep it isolated from what it judges, and audit it. Then rebuild the task set from real migration tickets rather than eleven remembered ones, and fold every production failure back into it. Trajectory scoring is worth adding after that, to explain the failures the gate now catches. Use the leaderboard only to shortlist the two coding models, and decide between them on your own tasks once the gate exists. Asking one model whether the diff looks good is the practice that failed, and the unit tests passing on every task is not evidence of anything — the agent wrote them.
cases.note: Three cases, three first moves: fix what you measure with, fix the shape of what you measure, and actually run the work. What they share is that the reassuring number in each — 94%, 91%, every unit test passing — was measuring something nobody had checked was worth measuring.

quiz: Your agent passes 92% of the release suite, but support tickets about wrong refunds are rising. Traces show many passing runs first called issue_refund with the wrong currency, then corrected it. Which evaluation would have caught this?
Add more tasks to the system-level suite
Process-level eval of tool calls and arguments
A public benchmark such as τ-bench
RAG context recall
The outcome looked right, so system-level eval passed it. The damage happened in an intermediate step with side effects. Scoring each tool call and its arguments exposes it.
A pairwise judge prefers response A 70% of the time. When you swap the order, it prefers whichever response is shown first. What is happening?
Position bias
Verbosity bias
Self-preference
The judge is well calibrated
Preferring whatever appears first is position bias. Run both orders and only count consistent wins.
Your RAG bot answers confidently but wrongly. Faithfulness is 0.95 and context recall is 0.40. What do you fix first?
The generation prompt
Retrieval
The judge model
Temperature
High faithfulness means the model sticks to what it was given. Low recall means it was given the wrong material, so fix retrieval first.
A coding agent says it built a pipeline that meets 12 requirements. Which technique verifies this most reliably?
LLM-as-a-Judge reading the agent's final message
Agent-as-a-Judge that runs the code and inspects outputs
The model's SWE-bench score
BLEU against a reference README
Only a judge that can run and inspect the work gathers real evidence. Reading the agent's own summary just checks its claims.
You ran 50 tasks 5 times each. 45 tasks passed at least once, but only 36 passed all 5 runs. What is pass^5, and what does it tell you?
0.90: the agent is reliable
0.72: the agent is inconsistent
0.18: the agent mostly fails
0.45: half the runs failed
pass^5 = 36 ÷ 50 = 0.72. The gap from 0.90 (pass@5) shows many tasks succeed only sometimes.
Your judge agrees with human pass/fail labels only 58% of the time. What's the best next step?
Switch to a 1–10 scale for more nuance
Rewrite the rubric with anchored examples and re-measure agreement
Trust it, since it's cheaper than people
Average it with a string-match metric
58% on a binary task is close to chance. A clearer rubric with examples usually fixes it; finer scales tend to make judges less consistent.
Model X tops SWE-bench Verified, but on 60 of your own issues it trails model Y. What should drive your choice?
The public scoreboard
Your internal eval
An average of both
Pick X and fine-tune it later
Benchmarks shortlist; your own tasks, harness and constraints decide.
Which metric needs a ground-truth reference answer?
Faithfulness
Answer relevancy
Context recall
Toxicity
Context recall checks whether retrieved context covers the facts in a reference answer, so it needs one. Faithfulness only compares the answer with the retrieved context.
An agent solves a task in 14 tool calls; the reference path needs 5. The task succeeded. What does process-level eval add?
Nothing: success is 100%
Step efficiency of 5 ÷ 14 ≈ 0.36
Step efficiency of 14 ÷ 5 = 2.8
A pass^k of 0.36
Efficiency = optimal ÷ actual steps = 0.36. A success that costs almost 3× the necessary steps is a cost and latency problem.
You want the release gate to fail if cost per resolved ticket jumps 40%, even when success holds. Which technique owns this?
System-level eval
Process-level eval
LLM-as-a-Judge
Benchmark suites
Cost per success is an end-to-end outcome metric, reported alongside success rate and latency in system-level eval.

system.t: You ran 4 tasks × 3 trials. T1 ✓✓✓, T2 ✓✗✓, T3 ✓✓✓, T4 ✗✗✓. What is pass^3?
system.a: Success rate over all runs = 9 of 12 = 75%. pass^3 counts tasks that passed all 3 trials: T1 and T3, so 2 ÷ 4 = 0.5. The gap between 75% and 0.5 is flakiness.
iv: Why isn't a single success-rate number enough for an agent release gate?

Agents are non-deterministic and cost money per run. Report success over repeated trials (pass^k for consistency), cost per success and p95 latency. A new version can keep the same success rate while doubling cost or becoming flaky.
How do you build a golden task set for system-level eval?

Sample real, anonymized requests across intents and difficulty, add known edge cases and past failures, and give each task a programmatically checkable end state such as a database row, a file or a passing test. Keep 50–200 tasks, version the set, and add every new production failure to it.
mis: Grading only the final message with string matching
Check the end state in code: the order status, the file, the test result
Running each task once
Run 3–5 trials and report pass^k alongside the average

process.t: Reference path: [search, get_account, refund]. Actual: [search, get_account, get_account, lookup_fx, refund]. What is the step efficiency? Does the in-order match pass?
process.a: Efficiency = 3 ÷ 5 = 0.6. The in-order match passes because search, get_account and refund appear in that order with extra steps allowed. An exact match fails.
iv: What's the difference between exact, in-order and any-order trajectory matching?

Exact requires the same tool sequence. In-order requires the reference steps to appear in order but allows extra steps. Any-order only requires every reference step to appear somewhere. Stricter matching penalizes valid alternatives, so choose per task.
How would you debug an agent that succeeds but costs 3× more than expected?

Trace every step, then look at step efficiency and redundant calls per tool. The cause is usually a vague tool description, missing information in a tool result, or no clear stop condition, and each shows up in process-level scores.
mis: Requiring an exact match to one reference path
Use in-order or any-order matching, or a per-step rubric
Logging tool names without arguments and results
Trace arguments and results for every span

llmjudge.t: Your judge and a human labelled 10 answers pass/fail and agreed on 8. What is the percent agreement, and why can it overstate the judge's quality?
llmjudge.a: Agreement = 8 ÷ 10 = 80%. Percent agreement ignores agreement by chance: if most labels are “pass”, a judge that always says pass agrees often. Cohen's κ corrects for chance.
iv: Which biases affect LLM judges, and how do you reduce them?

Position bias (run both orders), verbosity bias (state in the rubric that length earns nothing), and self-preference (judge with a different model family). Always calibrate against a human-labelled sample.
Why prefer binary or 3-point scales over 1–10?
Models are inconsistent at fine-grained scores; the same answer drifts between 6 and 8. Coarse scales with anchored examples are more repeatable and easier to calibrate against people.
mis: Asking for the score before the reasoning
Ask for reasoning first, then the score
Trusting the judge without human spot checks
Hand-label 50–100 cases and re-check agreement regularly

agentjudge.t: Requirements: R1 builds (pass), R2 tests run (pass), R3 depends on R2 and writes CSV (pass), R4 depends on R3 and plots (fail), R5 writes docs (fail). What is the requirement satisfaction rate, in %?
agentjudge.a: 3 of 5 = 60%. With dependency-aware scoring, R3 counts because its prerequisite R2 passed; R4 fails on its own evidence.
iv: When would you choose Agent-as-a-Judge over LLM-as-a-Judge?

When correctness can only be confirmed by acting: running code, opening files, querying outputs. LLM-as-a-Judge reads text; an agent judge gathers evidence. It's worth the extra cost for long, artifact-producing tasks.
How do you stop a judge agent from damaging what it evaluates?
Run it in a sandbox with read-only mounts and tools, no network or write credentials, and time limits, and require an evidence citation for every verdict.
mis: Giving the judge the same write tools as the agent
Read-only tools in an isolated sandbox
Accepting verdicts without evidence
Require a file, output or log citation for each verdict

rag.t: An answer makes 5 claims; 4 are supported by the retrieved chunks. The reference answer has 4 facts, and the retrieved context covers 3. What is the faithfulness score?
rag.a: Faithfulness = 4 ÷ 5 = 0.8. Context recall = 3 ÷ 4 = 0.75. Both halves need work, but the unsupported claim is the more urgent risk.
iv: A RAG system gives wrong answers. How do you tell whether retrieval or generation is at fault?

Score them separately. Low context recall or precision means retrieval missed. High recall with low faithfulness means the model is ignoring or going beyond its context. Fix the half the metrics point to.
What is the RAG triad?
Context relevance (is the retrieved context on topic), groundedness (is the answer supported by it) and answer relevance (does it address the question). TruLens popularized the term.
mis: Measuring only end-to-end answer accuracy
Score retrieval and generation separately
Testing with questions written from the documents
Use real user questions, which are messier and expose retrieval gaps

bench.t: Model A resolves 62% of SWE-bench Verified at $0.40 per task. Model B resolves 58% at $0.10. Over 1,000 tasks, what is B's cost per resolved issue, in $?
bench.a: A: $400 ÷ 620 ≈ $0.65 per resolved issue. B: $100 ÷ 580 ≈ $0.17. B is about 4× cheaper per resolved issue for 4 points less.
iv: Why can't you choose a model on scoreboard scores alone?
Benchmarks can be contaminated or saturated, run with harness settings unlike yours, and cover different tasks. Use them to shortlist, then decide with a private eval on your own tasks.
What does SWE-bench Verified measure?

Whether an agent can resolve real GitHub issues from Python repositories: its patch must make the failing tests pass without breaking others. Verified is a 500-issue subset that human annotators checked.
mis: Comparing scores produced with different harnesses
Use the official harness and report settings
Quoting only the pass rate
Report pass@1 with cost and run time

evaldata.t: Suraksha General’s claims assistant scores about 85% on real traffic. How many test cases are needed for a 95% margin of ±3 percentage points? Use n = 1.96² × p(1 − p) ÷ margin².
evaldata.a: n = 3.8416 × 0.85 × 0.15 ÷ 0.03² = 0.4898 ÷ 0.0009 ≈ 544.2, so round up to 545 cases. Halving the margin to ±1.5 points needs four times as many, about 2,177.
iv: How would you build an evaluation dataset for a production agent?

Sample real traffic, tickets and cases subject experts flag, after redacting personal data. Stratify by intent, language and risk with a minimum per stratum, and add edge and adversarial cases; use synthetic cases only to fill gaps, after expert review. Label with a written rubric, two annotators on at least a sample, measure agreement and adjudicate. Size it for the margin you need, version it, keep a holdout, and add new production failures every cycle.
Your agent went from 84% to 87% on a 150-case test set. Is it better?

Not provably. At about 85% and 150 cases, one score has a margin near ±5.7 points, and the difference between two scores about ±8. A 3-point gain is inside that. Check paired results on the same cases, look at which cases flipped, and add cases, especially in the slices that matter, before claiming a win.
mis: Testing only on synthetic questions generated from documentation
Sample real production traffic, stratify it, and keep synthetic cases to reviewed gap-fillers
Tuning prompts against the same test set until the score rises
Keep a holdout you never tune on, and refresh the set with new failures each release

usersim.t: An agent succeeds on a scenario 71% of the time, independently per run. What is pass^4, the chance that all 4 runs succeed, as a percentage?
iv: Why simulate users with an LLM instead of scripting turns?

Scripted turns do not react to what the agent says, so an agent that forgets to ask for a detail still passes. An LLM user with a goal and hidden details behaves like a real customer and exposes those gaps.
What is pass^k and why report it?
The probability that all k independent runs of a scenario succeed. Users meet the agent many times; an agent right 71% of the time succeeds on all four tries only about 25% of the time.
mis: Letting the simulator reveal every detail at once
Instruct it to reveal hidden details only when asked
Judging by transcript wording
Check the end state in the backend

pairwise.t: B wins 56% of 800 paired comparisons. What is the half-width of the 95% interval, in percentage points, using 1.96 × √(p(1−p)/n)?
iv: How do you decide whether a new prompt is better?

Run both on the same fixed question set, judge each pair in both orders, compute B’s win rate with a 95% interval, and ship only if the interval is above 50%. Choose the sample size beforehand from the smallest gain worth detecting.
Why judge both orders?
LLM judges have position bias. Swapping the order and treating split verdicts as ties cancels the bias; the split rate also shows how consistent the judge is.
mis: Stopping when B first looks ahead
Fix n in advance and run to the end
Comparing two separate averages
Use paired results on the same questions

gloss: pass^k
Share of tasks an agent solves in all k repeated trials. Measures consistency; stricter than pass@k.
pass@k
Share of tasks solved in at least one of k attempts. Measures capability, not reliability.
p95 latency
The time within which 95% of requests finish; tracks the slow tail users notice.
trajectory
The sequence of steps, tool calls and results an agent produces while solving a task.
golden set
A fixed, versioned set of tasks with known correct outcomes, used to compare versions.
rubric
Written grading criteria, ideally with an example for each score level.
Cohen's κ
Agreement between two raters corrected for chance: 1 is perfect, 0 is chance level.
faithfulness
Share of an answer's claims supported by the retrieved context.
context recall
Share of the reference answer's facts covered by the retrieved context.
context precision
Whether relevant chunks are ranked near the top of the retrieved list.
contamination
Benchmark items leaking into a model's training data, inflating its score.
span
One timed unit in a trace, such as a single LLM or tool call, with its inputs and outputs.
stratified sampling
Sampling separately from each group, such as intent, language or risk tier, so small but important groups are represented instead of being left to chance.
inter-annotator agreement
How often two people labelling the same cases agree, usually reported as a percentage and a chance-corrected score such as Cohen’s κ.
adjudication
Settling each case where annotators disagree, usually by a senior reviewer, and updating the rubric where it was unclear.
margin of error
Half the width of a confidence interval; for a 95% interval on a rate, about 1.96 × √(p(1 − p) ÷ n).
user simulator
An LLM prompted to play a user from a scenario card during multi-turn evaluation.
scenario card
A test case for a simulated user: persona, goal, hidden details, stop rule and expected end state.
pass^k
The probability that all k runs of the same task succeed; a reliability measure.
win rate
Share of paired comparisons a version wins, with ties usually counted as half.
position bias
A judge’s tendency to favour an answer because of its slot, first or second.
Bradley–Terry model
A statistical model that turns pairwise win and loss counts into a ranking of strengths.

llmjudge.note: An LLM judge can label preference pairs at scale, but its biases, such as preferring longer answers, pass straight into DPO.

rag.name: Query Rewriting and HyDE

rag.name: Hybrid Search
rag.note: Hybrid search is a common fix for low context recall.

rag.name: Output Guardrails
rag.note: Output grounding checks apply the faithfulness idea from RAG evaluation at run time.

rag.name: Prompt vs RAG vs Fine-Tune
rag.note: If the gap is knowledge rather than behaviour, fix retrieval and measure it with RAG evals before considering tuning.

rag.name: Citations and Grounded Answers
rag.note: RAG evaluation measures faithfulness across a test set; citations make it checkable in every answer.

rag.name: Multilingual and Code-Mixed Embeddings
rag.note: RAG evaluation should report retrieval recall per language slice, or a strong English slice can hide a failing Hindi one.

rag.name: Grounding and Hallucination Checks
rag.note: The same faithfulness scores used offline in RAG metrics can run online as a gate.

process.name: Agent Execution Graphs
process.note: Execution graphs make the trajectory explicit, which makes step-level scoring easier.

process.name: ReAct Loop
process.note: Process evaluation grades the ReAct trajectory step by step, not just the final answer.

process.name: Function Calling Basics
process.note: Process evaluation scores tool calls after the fact; function calling is how each call is made and returned.

process.name: OpenTelemetry GenAI Tracing
process.note: Process-level evaluation grades the steps of a run, and traces are where those steps are recorded.

system.name: Model Routing and Tiering
system.note: Route traffic to a small model only after system-level eval shows it passes on that traffic.

system.name: Online Evals and Drift Alerts
system.note: System-level evals run offline before release; online evals keep scoring the same qualities on live traffic after it.

system.name: Canary Releases and Prompt Flags
system.note: Offline system-level evals are the gate before a canary; the canary is the last check on live traffic.

system.name: Prompt Templates and Regression Tests
system.note: A golden-case suite for prompts is a system-level eval run on every change.

system.name: Evaluate Before and After Tuning
system.note: Before-and-after evaluation of a tuned model is a system-level eval on a clean held-out set, plus regression suites.

system.name: Model and System Cards
system.note: A system card is only as honest as the evals behind it; report system-level results by segment.

system.name: Eval Datasets
system.note: System-level eval gates releases on a golden set; this technique is how that set is sourced, stratified, labelled, sized and kept fresh.

system.name: User Simulation for Multi-Turn Agents
system.note: End-state checks are system-level eval applied after a whole conversation.

bench.note: OSWorld and WebArena are benchmark suites: useful for choosing, not a substitute for evals on your own tasks.
